text: Luis Buñuel and Salvador Dalí's 'Un Chien Andalou' (1929) — whose opening scene features an eye being slit with a razor — remains the defining Surrealist film; its juxtaposition of images follows dream logic rather than narrative causality, and Buñuel later said the film was designed specifically to have no rational interpretation.

Nollywood — the Nigerian film industry — became the world's second-largest film producer by volume (over 2,500 films per year) by the early 2010s, overtaking Hollywood and surpassed only by Bollywood; its low-budget direct-to-video model, using consumer digital cameras and 10-day shooting schedules, demonstrated that viable commercial cinema can exist outside the Hollywood financial model.

The experimental film 'Man with a Movie Camera' (1929) by Dziga Vertov — a day in Soviet urban life with no actors, intertitles, or narrative — pioneered nearly every avant-garde film technique: split-screen, freeze frame, slow motion, fast motion, reverse motion, and extreme close-ups; voted the greatest documentary of all time by the BFI in 2014.

The IMAX format, developed in Canada and first shown at Expo '70 in Osaka, uses film 10 times the size of standard 35mm; Christopher Nolan's commitment to shooting with IMAX cameras for 'The Dark Knight' (2008) and subsequent films revived the format's theatrical use and established a premium for IMAX screenings that theater chains now command at 40–50% above standard ticket prices.

Andrei Tarkovsky's 'Stalker' (1979), 'Solaris' (1972), and 'Mirror' (1975) established a contemplative cinema of long takes, memory, and metaphysical yearning that Tarkovsky theorized in his book 'Sculpting in Time' (1986); his influence on directors including Terrence Malick, Lars von Trier, and Carlos Reygadas constitutes one of cinema's most significant philosophical lineages.

The Hong Kong action cinema of the 1970s–90s, pioneered by Bruce Lee and perfected by Jackie Chan's 'Police Story' series and John Woo's 'Heroic Bloodshed' films ('The Killer,' 1989; 'Hard Boiled,' 1992), developed a kinetic choreography of violence that directly influenced Quentin Tarantino, the Wachowskis ('The Matrix'), and the Marvel Cinematic Universe's fight choreography.

Spaghetti Westerns (Italian-made American Westerns shot in Spain, 1960s–1970s), led by Sergio Leone's 'Dollar Trilogy' and 'Once Upon a Time in the West' (1968), reinterpreted the American Western with European cynicism, operatic violence, and extreme close-ups of eyes; Ennio Morricone's distinctive scores using unconventional instruments (electric guitar, whistling, gunshots) became equally iconic.

The term 'cinéma vérité' — coined by Edgar Morin and Jean Rouch for their landmark documentary 'Chronicle of a Summer' (1961) — refers to a French tradition distinct from American direct cinema; while direct cinema tried to observe unobtrusively, cinéma vérité deliberately provoked subjects with challenging questions to reveal truth through confrontation.

Wong Kar-wai's '2046' (2004) and 'In the Mood for Love' (2000), shot by Christopher Doyle using available light in cramped Hong Kong apartment corridors, developed a lyrical aesthetic of memory, longing, and temporal displacement — with multiple shoots over five years and improvised scripts — that made Wong the defining auteur of late Hong Kong cinema.

The Marx Brothers' anarchic comedies for Paramount ('Duck Soup,' 1933) and MGM ('A Night at the Opera,' 1935) deconstructed authority, narrative, and the fourth wall with verbal wit (Groucho), visual poetry (Harpo), and Italian operatic parody (Chico); their influence extends to Monty Python, the Zucker-Abrahams-Zucker team ('Airplane!'), and the entire tradition of anti-authoritarian screen comedy.

The casting of unknown actors in major roles has produced some of cinema's most celebrated performances: George Lucas cast then-unknown Harrison Ford, Carrie Fisher, and Mark Hamill in 'Star Wars'; Francis Ford Coppola used mostly non-professional actors in 'The Godfather' (opposite Al Pacino and Marlon Brando); and Richard Linklater used the same non-professional cast over 12 years in 'Boyhood' (2014).

The 'Method Acting' technique, derived from Konstantin Stanislavski's system and taught in the United States by Lee Strasberg at the Actors Studio (founded 1947), trained Marlon Brando, James Dean, Al Pacino, Dustin Hoffman, and Robert De Niro; De Niro's extreme preparation — learning to play saxophone, boxing professionally, and gaining 60 lbs for 'Raging Bull' (1980) — exemplifies Method's demands.

The 'Kuleshov lesson' that studios took from early Soviet cinema led to the 'coverage' approach to Hollywood production: filming every scene from multiple angles to allow editors maximum flexibility in post-production; this system — shooting the same scene 5–10 times from different distances and angles — is the opposite of Kubrick's or Tarkovsky's single-angle approach.

The Hollywood blacklist (1947–1960), during which the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) investigated alleged Communist infiltration of the film industry, ended the careers of over 300 writers, directors, and actors including Charlie Chaplin, Dalton Trumbo, and the 'Hollywood Ten'; Trumbo wrote 'Roman Holiday' (1953) under a pseudonym, which won an Oscar — returned to him posthumously in 1993.

The Hays Code (Motion Picture Production Code), adopted in 1930 and enforced from 1934 to 1968 by the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America, banned depictions of interracial romance, drug trafficking, homosexuality, excessive violence, and nudity; filmmakers developed sophisticated systems of implication and symbol to convey censored content, producing what many consider Hollywood's most artistically inventive period.

The MPAA film rating system (G, PG, PG-13, R, NC-17), established in 1968 as the Hays Code collapsed, has been criticized for rating sexual content more strictly than violence; the introduction of 'PG-13' in 1984 (following parental outcry over violence in 'Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom' and 'Gremlins') became the dominant commercial sweet spot for Hollywood blockbusters.

Edward Muybridge's 1878 photographic sequence proving that a galloping horse momentarily has all four hooves off the ground — commissioned by railroad magnate Leland Stanford to settle a bet — is considered a foundational moment of both scientific photography and proto-cinema; Muybridge later invented the zoopraxiscope (1879), one of the first devices to project moving images.

The Lumière Brothers' first public screening of films to a paying audience at the Grand Café in Paris (December 28, 1895) is conventionally considered cinema's birth; their 'Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat' reportedly caused audience members to flee in terror, believing the train was real — though historians now believe this story is largely mythological.

Nickelodeons — small storefront theaters showing short films for a nickel — spread across American cities between 1905 and 1915, with over 10,000 operating nationwide by 1910; they provided cheap entertainment for working-class and immigrant audiences, and their demographics shaped early film content toward action, comedy, and melodrama rather than literary adaptation.

The Motion Picture Patents Company (MPPC, 'Edison Trust'), founded in 1908 by Thomas Edison to monopolize the American film industry through patent control, drove independent producers to Southern California — where the distance from Edison's New Jersey lawyers made enforcement difficult; Hollywood's founding as a film center was thus partly a consequence of legal evasion.

The 'Picture Palace' era (1910s–1950s) saw the construction of lavishly decorated movie theaters — including Grauman's Chinese Theatre (1927) and Radio City Music Hall (1932) — designed to make film attendance a theatrical event; the Palace circuit's decline with television led to their conversion to multiplex cinemas in the 1970s, with many demolished or converted to retail spaces.

The drive-in theater, invented in New Jersey in 1933 by Richard Hollingshead, reached its American peak in 1958 with 4,063 theaters; the format catered to suburban families and teenagers and was associated with exploitation films, horror, and B-movies; fewer than 300 remain operating in the US today, though the COVID-19 pandemic briefly revived interest in the 2020 outdoor exhibition format.

Alfred Hitchcock's 'Rear Window' (1954) — in which a photographer confined to his apartment watches his neighbors through a telephoto lens and comes to believe he has witnessed a murder — is both a masterful thriller and a meditation on film spectatorship itself; Laura Mulvey's 1975 essay 'Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema' used Hitchcock's work to develop 'the male gaze' concept in film theory.

Werner Herzog and Klaus Kinski's stormy collaboration produced 'Aguirre, the Wrath of God' (1972), 'Fitzcarraldo' (1982) — shot with a real 320-ton steamship being hauled over a Peruvian mountain — and 'Nosferatu the Vampyre' (1979); Herzog's documentary 'My Best Fiend' (1999) detailed their mutual terrorizing relationship while acknowledging that Kinski's madness produced greatness.

The screen test — a filmed audition where actors perform scenes to assess how they appear on camera — has produced legendary stories: Grace Kelly's test for 'Mogambo' launched her Hollywood career; Marilyn Monroe failed her initial screen test at Columbia Pictures; and Fred Astaire's famous 1928 test report allegedly stated 'Can't sing, can't act, slightly bald, can dance a little.'

The Dogville experiment — Lars von Trier's 'Dogville' (2003) shot entirely on a bare warehouse floor with chalk outlines indicating walls and props — demonstrated that cinema's power of suggestion can make an audience see non-existent environments; this 'poor cinema' approach influenced theatrical film and recalled Bertolt Brecht's alienation effect.

The Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU), launched with 'Iron Man' (2008), redefined Hollywood's business model through interconnected 'universe' storytelling spanning 30+ films; its cumulative worldwide gross exceeded $30 billion by 2023, making it the highest-grossing film franchise in history — a model Disney also applied to Star Wars, and Warner Bros. attempted with DC.

The Nouvelle Vague director Jean-Luc Godard (1930–2022) never stopped experimenting: from 'Breathless' (1960) to 'Film Socialisme' (2010), shot on a consumer camcorder; his 'Histoire(s) du Cinéma' (1988–1998), an 8-part video essay arguing that cinema failed to document the Holocaust, is considered one of the most ambitious theoretical works ever produced in the film medium.

The Laemmle family's Universal Pictures, founded in 1912, holds the distinction of being the oldest surviving Hollywood studio; its 'Universal Monsters' franchise (1931–1956) was cinema's first shared universe — characters crossed between films years before Marvel — and included Dracula, Frankenstein, the Mummy, the Wolf Man, and the Invisible Man.

The 'long lens compression' effect — using telephoto lenses of 200mm or longer to make distant objects appear closer to foreground elements than they are — creates the visual sensation of a packed, compressed space used in news coverage of crowds or in films wanting to emphasize congestion and surveillance; it is contrasted with wide-angle 'distorted' perspective that makes spaces feel larger.

The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences' film library has been digitally scanning and preserving over 250,000 films, stills, posters, and scripts since 2012; in 2024 its new $482 million Academy Museum of Motion Pictures in Los Angeles became the largest museum in North America dedicated to the history and science of filmmaking.

The 'golden age of television' (2000–present), inaugurated by 'The Sopranos' (HBO, 1999–2007) and expanded by 'The Wire,' 'Mad Men,' and 'Breaking Bad,' attracted major film directors and cinematographers to television, raising its visual and narrative ambition to cinematic levels; streaming platforms' binge-watching model further transformed storytelling rhythms, effectively making multi-hour series the new novel.

The 'magic lantern,' a projection device using painted or photographic glass slides illuminated by candlelight or oil lamp, was the dominant form of projected image entertainment from the 17th century until cinema replaced it in the early 20th century; magic lantern shows included lectures, ghost projections ('Pepper's Ghost'), and narrative stories, making them a direct predecessor of both cinema and the PowerPoint presentation.

The 'Zoetrope,' invented by William George Horner in 1834, created the illusion of motion by viewing sequential drawings through slots in a spinning drum; it preceded film by 60 years and is one of several 'philosophical toys' (along with the Phenakistoscope, Praxinoscope, and Flipbook) that demonstrated persistence of vision and the neurological basis of cinema.

The 'aspect ratio' of a film — the proportional relationship between its width and height — has evolved from the 1.33:1 ('Academy ratio') established by Edison in 1892 through the 1.85:1 American widescreen standard and 2.39:1 anamorphic CinemaScope to 9:16 vertical video optimized for smartphone screens; each shift reflects changing exhibition technology and audience viewing habits.

Henri Cartier-Bresson's concept of 'the decisive moment' (l'instant décisif), articulated in his 1952 collection, holds that photography captures the split second when form and content perfectly coincide; Cartier-Bresson co-founded Magnum Photos (1947), the world's first photographer-owned cooperative agency, which set the standard for photojournalism ethics and documentary photography.

Dorothea Lange's 'Migrant Mother' (1936), taken for the Farm Security Administration during the Great Depression and showing Florence Owens Thompson with her children, is the most reproduced documentary photograph in history; Thompson did not learn of her fame until 1978 and reportedly received no compensation, raising questions about documentary subjects' rights that still inform photography ethics.

Robert Capa's 'Falling Soldier' (1936), purporting to show the exact moment a Republican soldier is shot during the Spanish Civil War, remains photography's most debated image; its authenticity has been disputed since the 1970s, but the debate itself — about whether staged or manipulated photographs can be considered documentary — shaped modern photojournalism's ethical standards.

The 'f-stop' system for measuring lens aperture — where each stop doubles or halves the amount of light entering the camera — was standardized in 1900 by the Royal Photographic Society; the counterintuitive numbering (lower f-numbers = wider apertures = more light) confuses beginning photographers but reflects the mathematical relationship between focal length and aperture diameter.

The 35mm film format, standardized by Thomas Edison and William Dickson in 1892, became the universal standard for both still photography and cinema for over a century; Kodak's introduction of the Leica-compatible 35mm cassette in the 1920s enabled Cartier-Bresson and other street photographers to work discreetly, creating the entire tradition of candid small-camera photography.

Ansel Adams developed the Zone System with Fred Archer at the Art Center School of Los Angeles in 1939–1941, providing photographers a systematic method to previsualise exposure in 11 zones from pure black to pure white; Adams's monumental photographs of Yosemite, Half Dome, and the American West became the defining images of wilderness photography and influenced the modern environmental movement.

The 'New Topographics' photography exhibition at the George Eastman House in 1975 — featuring Robert Adams, Lewis Baltz, and others — presented deadpan photographs of suburban tract homes, parking lots, and industrial sites, deliberately refusing the romanticism of landscape photography; it established conceptual photography as a legitimate fine art form and influenced a generation of artists.

Sebastião Salgado's 'Workers' (1993) and 'Exodus' (2000), projects documenting global labor and mass migration across seven years of fieldwork on every continent, represent photography's most ambitious longform documentary projects; his subsequent project 'Genesis' (2013) — photographing 32 territories where nature exists untouched — was accompanied by a reforestation project replanting 2 million trees in Brazil.

The daguerreotype, introduced by Louis Daguerre in 1839, was the first commercially viable photographic process, using a highly polished silver plate to produce unique, sharply detailed images; Napoleon III's photographer Nadar (Gaspard-Félix Tournachon) used the daguerreotype to create the first aerial photographs from a hot-air balloon over Paris in 1858.

Kodachrome, Kodak's reversal color film introduced in 1935 (popularized in Paul Simon's 1973 song), was manufactured for 74 years before being discontinued in 2009; its distinctive, saturated color rendition shaped Americans' visual memory of the mid-20th century, and the last roll was processed in Parsons, Kansas in January 2011 by the world's final licensed Kodachrome lab.

The Polaroid instant camera, invented by Edwin Land in 1947, produced a self-developing photograph in about a minute; Land's SX-70 (1972) was the first folding SLR instant camera and became an artistic medium for Andy Warhol and David Hockney; after Polaroid's bankruptcy in 2001, the Impossible Project (now Polaroid Originals) revived instant film production in 2008.

The first digital camera was invented by Kodak engineer Steven Sasson in 1975 — a 3.6-kg prototype recording 0.01 megapixel black-and-white images to a cassette tape in 23 seconds; Kodak patented it but, fearing it would cannibalize film sales, did not commercialize it, a business decision that contributed to Kodak's eventual bankruptcy in 2012 when digital photography destroyed its core business.

Weegee (Arthur Fellig), a New York press photographer of the 1930s–40s, used a police radio and darkroom in his car trunk to photograph crime scenes, fires, and accidents within minutes of their occurrence; his book 'Naked City' (1945) defined urban tabloid photography and directly inspired Jules Dassin's noir 'The Naked City' (1948) and the entire tradition of New York crime photography.

Diane Arbus's photographs of 'freaks,' twins, nudists, transvestites, and mentally disabled individuals in the 1960s deliberately violated conventions of sympathetic documentary photography; her 1972 retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art remains the most visited photography exhibition in MoMA's history, and her 1971 suicide made her images posthumously iconic.

Nick Ut's 'Napalm Girl' (1972) — showing 9-year-old Kim Phúc running naked from a napalm attack in Vietnam — won the 1973 Pulitzer Prize and is credited with hastening US withdrawal from Vietnam; AP's initial hesitation to distribute the image due to nudity was overridden, and the photograph became one of the most debated examples of the tension between journalistic impact and ethical restraint.

The 'decisive moment' philosophy of street photography contrasts with the 'constructed' photography of artists like Jeff Wall — who creates large-format, transparently backlit photographs (Cibachromes) that look like film stills but are elaborately staged; Wall's 'A Sudden Gust of Wind (after Hokusai)' (1993) took over a year and hundreds of photographs to complete, blurring the documentary/fiction boundary.

The history of color photography follows several parallel tracks: autochromes (Lumière brothers, 1907), Dufaycolor (1930s), Kodachrome (1935), Ektachrome (1946), and color negative film (1941); the transition to consumer color printing, which made color snapshots the household norm, occurred only in the late 1970s — decades after color photography was technically possible.

The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, has produced some of the most viewed and reproduced images in human history — including the 'Pillars of Creation' (1995) and the Hubble Deep Field (1996, showing approximately 3,000 galaxies in a patch of sky previously thought empty); the Space Telescope Science Institute processes Hubble's data into false-color composite images that make invisible electromagnetic radiation visually comprehensible.

The 'event horizon telescope' — a global network of radio telescopes synchronized to create a virtual Earth-sized telescope — captured the first direct image of a black hole in 2019 (the supermassive black hole M87*, 55 million light-years away); the 2022 image of Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the center of our own Milky Way galaxy, required coordinating 8 telescopes across 4 continents.

The 'daguerreotype' made portraiture accessible to the middle classes for the first time — before photography, only the wealthy could afford painted portraits; by 1853, approximately 3 million daguerreotypes were being produced annually in the United States alone, representing one of history's fastest adoptions of a new visual technology.

Alfred Stieglitz's 291 Gallery in New York (1905–1917) was the first gallery in America to exhibit photographs as fine art alongside Matisse, Picasso, and Cézanne; his journal Camera Work (1903–1917) and the Photo-Secession movement he founded established photography's claim to artistic status in America, a claim still contested in fine art markets until the 1970s.

The 'selfie' — a photographic self-portrait taken with a smartphone's front-facing camera — was named Oxford Dictionaries' 2013 Word of the Year; its rise transformed portraiture, identity expression, and political image-making; Rembrandt, Van Gogh, and Frida Kahlo were predecessors in systematic self-portraiture, but Instagram's 2010 launch democratized the form to over a billion practitioners.

Margaret Bourke-White, hired as the first female photojournalist at Life magazine in 1936, photographed the opening of the Fort Peck Dam for Life's very first cover; during WWII she was the first female war photographer accredited by the US Army and the first photographer allowed into the liberated Buchenwald concentration camp, accompanied by General Patton.

The 'rule of thirds' — the compositional principle dividing the frame into a 3×3 grid and placing key elements at intersections — was first articulated by painter John Thomas Smith in 1797 and has been a foundational principle of photography education ever since; modern cameras and smartphones display grid overlays to assist application of the rule.

The 'pinhole camera' (camera obscura) — the oldest image-forming device, used by astronomers in the 11th century, by Leonardo da Vinci, and by artists for centuries as a drawing aid — operates on the principle that light passing through a tiny aperture projects an inverted image of the outside world; contemporary pinhole photographers use tin cans or matchboxes as cameras, exposures lasting hours or days.

The documentary photographer W. Eugene Smith's 'Country Doctor' (1948) in Life magazine — a 17-page photographic essay following a rural Colorado physician through 24-hour days — established the photo-essay as a narrative form with its own grammar of establishing shots, detail close-ups, environmental portraits, and decisive action moments that influenced television news and later multimedia journalism.

James Nachtwey, often cited as the greatest living war photographer, has covered virtually every major conflict since the 1980s from Lebanon to Rwanda to Iraq; his film 'War Photographer' (2001), directed by Christian Frei, won the Emmy Award for Best Documentary and raised fundamental questions about whether witnessing atrocity through a camera lens enables or prevents direct intervention.

The Medium Format camera system — using film or sensors significantly larger than 35mm (typically 44×33mm or 53.7×40.4mm) — produces images of exceptional resolution used in fashion, advertising, and fine art photography; the Hasselblad medium format camera was famously used on the Apollo lunar missions, and NASA images of the Moon were shot on Ektachrome film by Hasselblad cameras left on the lunar surface.

Nan Goldin's 'The Ballad of Sexual Dependency' (1986) — a slideshow of 700 images depicting her friends in New York's underground LGBTQ community, drug users, drag queens, and intimate sexual moments — is considered the most influential photo book of the late 20th century; Goldin's 2022 campaign against the Sackler family's role in the opioid crisis led major museums worldwide to remove the Sackler name.

The 'decisive moment' in cinema translates into the choice of when to cut — editor Anne Coates cut 'Lawrence of Arabia' (1962) with the famous match cut from Lawrence blowing out a match to the sun rising over the desert, widely cited as the most beautiful cut in film history; Coates also edited 'The Elephant Man,' 'Out of Sight,' and 'Fifty Shades of Grey.'

The 'Dutch angle' — tilting the camera on its horizontal axis to create a canted, disorienting composition — was popularized in expressionist films to convey psychological disturbance; its use in 'The Third Man' (1949), 'Batman' (1966 TV series), and virtually every film depicting corruption or villainy has made it one of cinema's most recognizable visual shorthand devices.

The 'Dolly zoom' (also called the 'Vertigo effect' or 'Zolly shot') — simultaneously zooming in and dollying backward so the subject remains the same size while the background zooms away — was invented by Irmin Roberts for Hitchcock's 'Vertigo' (1958); its psychological effect of spatial dislocation was later used by Spielberg in 'Jaws' (1975) and has become a standard cinematic vocabulary for emotional shock.

The 'Ken Burns Effect' — a slow pan or zoom across a still photograph used to suggest time's passage, popularized in Burns's 'The Civil War' (1990, PBS) — is now a default setting in iMovie and Final Cut Pro, making it the most democratically distributed film technique in history; Burns's documentary style (expert interviews, archive photographs, actor voiceovers) influenced virtually all American historical documentary television.

The video nasties controversy in the UK (1982–1984), triggered by 'Video Recordings Act' (1984) after tabloid panic about violent VHS rentals including 'The Evil Dead,' 'Driller Killer,' and 'Cannibal Holocaust,' led to 72 films being banned outright and created Britain's classification system for home video; several films banned then are now widely available uncut.

The 'found footage' horror film format, popularized by 'The Blair Witch Project' (1999), uses the conceit that a character filmed the events; 'Cloverfield' (2008), 'REC' (2007), and 'Paranormal Activity' (2007 — made for $15,000, grossing $193 million) refined the format, which exploits cinema's indexical quality (the idea that photographs and films record reality) for horror effect.

The 'Lumière effect' — the capacity of cinema to present moving images as windows onto reality — distinguishes cinema from all previous visual arts; film theorist André Bazin argued in 'What Is Cinema?' (1951–1958) that cinema's fundamental nature is its ability to 'mummify change' — to capture actual time passing — which he saw as fulfilling humanity's age-old desire to preserve life against death.

Hitchcock's 'MacGuffin' — his term for a plot device that motivates characters and drives narrative but is otherwise irrelevant (the microfilm in 'North by Northwest,' the money in 'Psycho,' the Maltese Falcon in Huston's film) — became one of cinema's most important theoretical concepts; screenwriting guru Robert McKee considers it the most elegant formulation of narrative motivation in film theory.

The AFI's 2003 '100 Heroes and Villains' and '100 Greatest Films' lists, along with the annual Sight & Sound poll (conducted by the British Film Institute every decade since 1952), are cinema's most influential canons; the 2022 Sight & Sound poll — in which 1,639 critics voted — displaced 'Citizen Kane' after 60 years at the top, replacing it with Chantal Akerman's 'Jeanne Dielman' (1975), a landmark feminist film.

Chantal Akerman's 'Jeanne Dielman, 23, quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles' (1975) — a 3-hour 21-minute film depicting a housewife's domestic routines over three days in real time — uses duration as a political statement about the invisible labor of women; its promotion to the top of the 2022 Sight & Sound poll was celebrated by feminist film scholars as a long-overdue correction of the historically male-dominated canon.

The 'cinema of attractions' — a concept developed by film scholar Tom Gunning — describes early cinema (1895–1906) as primarily a medium of spectacle and display rather than narrative; early films showed acrobats, waves, trains, and exotic scenes as visual wonders; Gunning argues this mode never disappeared but coexists with narrative cinema, reappearing in action sequences, stunts, and special effects.

The 'Bechdel test' — named after cartoonist Alison Bechdel who introduced it in her 1985 comic 'Dykes to Watch Out For' — asks whether a film has at least two named female characters who talk to each other about something other than a man; although a low bar, fewer than 57% of films released in any given year meet all three criteria, revealing the persistent male-centrism of mainstream cinema.

The 'Auteur theory' — which holds that the director is the primary creative force or 'author' of a film — was challenged by structuralists and feminist critics who emphasized that cinema is a collaborative industrial art form; Peter Biskind's 'Easy Riders, Raging Bulls' (1998) documented how auteurism's celebration of individual vision often masked abusive behavior by directors given unchecked studio power.

Steven Spielberg's 'E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial' (1982), made for $10.5 million and grossing $435 million in its first run, was the highest-grossing film in history for 11 years until 'Jurassic Park' surpassed it; it popularized the 'point of view shot aligned with a child's eye level' — with all adults in the film shot from below the waist until the climax.

The 'exploitation film' tradition — low-budget films marketing forbidden content (sex, violence, drugs) that major studios avoided under the Hays Code — produced genuine artistic contributions alongside schlock; Roger Corman's AIP films launched the careers of Jack Nicholson, Francis Ford Coppola, Martin Scorsese, and Jonathan Demme, making Corman one of Hollywood history's most consequential talent scouts.

Eisenstein's 'Battleship Potemkin' (1925) contains the 'Odessa Steps' sequence — in which Tsarist troops massacre civilians, intercut with a baby carriage rolling down the steps — which is considered the most analyzed editing sequence in film history and the definitive demonstration of Soviet montage's emotional power; Brian De Palma reused it in 'The Untouchables' (1987) and 'Scarface' (1983).

The 'New Queer Cinema' movement (Bruce Babbitt's term, 1992), including Gus Van Sant's 'My Own Private Idaho' (1991), Todd Haynes's 'Poison' (1991), and Gregg Araki's 'The Living End' (1992), brought explicitly queer perspectives to independent American cinema in the AIDS crisis era; Haynes's subsequent 'Carol' (2015) and 'May December' (2023) demonstrate the movement's lasting artistic influence.

The 'slow cinema' movement — associated with directors Béla Tarr ('Sátántangó,' 1994, seven and a half hours), Carlos Reygadas, and Lav Diaz — uses extremely long takes, minimal dialogue, and real-time duration to challenge cinema's conventional rhythm; Tarr's 'Sátántangó' has 150 shots over 7.5 hours, averaging three minutes per shot, demanding a fundamentally different mode of attention from audiences.

The 'post-credit scene' — originally used by Marvel from 'Iron Man' (2008) to tease future films — has become standard practice across franchise filmmaking; 'The Avengers' (2012) added a comedic post-credit shawarma scene only 5 days before release, shot with Robert Downey Jr. still in partial Iron Man makeup, because the studio realized audiences expected it.

Brazil's Cinema Novo ('New Cinema,' 1960s–1970s), led by Glauber Rocha, Nelson Pereira dos Santos, and Ruy Guerra, applied neorealist and Nouvelle Vague techniques to Brazilian social reality; Rocha's manifesto 'An Aesthetic of Hunger' (1965) declared that Third Cinema must depict poverty not with sentimentality but with raw violence, influencing Latin American cinema for decades.

The Mexican 'Golden Age' of cinema (1936–1969), producing over 100 films per year and dominated by stars including María Félix, Pedro Infante, and Jorge Negrete, was Latin America's most commercially successful national cinema; it declined when government subsidies were withdrawn and Hollywood competition intensified, though directors like Emilio Fernández and cinematographer Gabriel Figueroa created visually distinctive works.

Ousmane Sembène, the 'father of African cinema,' made 'Borom Sarret' (1963, considered the first Sub-Saharan African feature), 'Black Girl' (1966), and 'Xala' (1975) — films that critiqued colonialism, post-independence corruption, and traditional patriarchy in Senegal; his insistence on filming in Wolof rather than French pioneered African-language cinema against the cultural dominance of European distribution.

The 'Mise-en-scène' approach to film criticism — developed by Cahiers du Cinéma in opposition to the primacy of editing — analyzes what is placed within the frame (lighting, staging, set design, costume, actor movement) rather than how shots are assembled; critics like V.F. Perkins ('Film as Film,' 1972) argued that meaning in cinema resides primarily in the relationship between elements within a single shot.

The 'snorkel lens' (Periscope lens) — a highly specialized camera system using a system of mirrors to place the lens inches from the ground or inside extremely small spaces — was developed by visual effects pioneers; it allowed filmmakers to create 'ant's-eye views,' car chase sequences with cameras embedded in the road, and tabletop miniature shots that appear to be full-scale environments.

George Méliès, the French stage magician who became cinema's first special effects pioneer, invented in-camera effects including double exposure, stop-motion, and substitution splices in over 500 films made between 1896 and 1913; Martin Scorsese's 'Hugo' (2011) — a love letter to Méliès — brought renewed attention to his contributions and led to a major restoration effort of surviving prints.

The 'motion capture' technology — recording an actor's movements using sensors and translating them to a digital character — was pioneered in James Cameron's 'Avatar' (2009), where Gollum in 'The Lord of the Rings' (Andy Serkis, 2001) demonstrated the potential for digital performance; the ongoing debate about whether motion-captured performances deserve Oscar consideration reflects cinema's evolving definition of 'acting.'

The 'Criterion Collection' — founded in 1984 to distribute important classic and contemporary films with supplementary materials — established the standard for home video curation; its distinctive spine numbers, commissioned artwork, and essay booklets transformed home cinema into a scholarly and aesthetic practice; as of 2024 it has released over 1,100 titles across Blu-ray, DVD, and its streaming channel.

The 'video essay' — a long-form critical analysis of cinema using the film medium itself — emerged as a significant form of film criticism on YouTube from around 2010; channels including Every Frame a Painting, kogonada, and Tony Zhou demonstrated that cinema could analyze cinema, producing works of criticism that are themselves cinematically constructed and often more widely viewed than written reviews.

The 'Hollywood Walk of Fame,' established in 1960 along Hollywood Boulevard and Vine Street in Los Angeles, has over 2,700 stars honoring performers, directors, producers, and fictional characters; the selection committee of the Hollywood Chamber of Commerce requires nominees to have a minimum of 5 years in the industry and a sponsoring company to pay the $75,000 cost of installation.

The film score composer Bernard Herrmann (1911–1975) revolutionized how music functions in film; his Hitchcock scores ('Psycho,' 1960; 'Vertigo,' 1958; 'North by Northwest,' 1959) abandoned the lush orchestral convention of the era for stark, percussive textures — the 'Psycho' shower scene strings, played by all-string orchestra, are considered the most effective horror music ever composed.

John Williams, who has composed scores for 'Jaws,' 'Star Wars,' 'Raiders of the Lost Ark,' 'Schindler's List,' 'E.T.,' 'Harry Potter,' 'Home Alone,' and many others, holds the record for most Oscar nominations for a living person (53 nominations, 5 wins); his leitmotif-based orchestral style, drawing on Wagnerian opera, revived symphonic film music at a time when pop scores dominated.

text: The 'immersive cinema' trend — including Secret Cinema's theatrical productions in which audiences inhabit the film's world, '4DX' theaters with moving seats and environmental effects, and virtual reality film experiences — represents a reversal of cinema's traditional passive spectatorship model; VR films shown at Sundance and Venice (2017–present) have raised questions about whether VR constitutes 'cinema' at all.

The 'New Argentine Cinema' (1990s–present), emerging after Argentina's economic collapse and featuring directors Pablo Trapero, Lucrecia Martel, and Lisandro Alonso, achieved international recognition for its minimalist aesthetics and unflinching depiction of social crisis; Martel's 'La Ciénaga' (2001) and 'The Headless Woman' (2008) are considered among the finest films of the 21st century.

The 'Romanian New Wave,' which emerged in the 2000s with Cristi Puiu's 'The Death of Mr. Lazarescu' (2005) and Cristian Mungiu's '4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days' (2007, Palme d'Or), applied rigorous long-take realism to the moral complexities of communist-era and post-communist Romanian life; the movement produced one of cinema's most concentrated national outpourings of quality filmmaking in a decade.

Terrence Malick's 'Days of Heaven' (1978), shot entirely by cinematographer Nestor Almendros (with Haskell Wexler) during the magic hour, required a 25-day shooting schedule to capture approximately 20 minutes of footage at dusk and dawn; it won the Cannes Best Director award and the Oscar for Cinematography, becoming the defining example of natural light as a philosophical filmmaking choice.

The 'New Chinese Cinema' of the 1980s–90s produced two internationally distinct waves: the Fifth Generation directors (Zhang Yimou, Chen Kaige) using visually sumptuous allegory, and Sixth Generation directors (Jia Zhangke, Wang Xiaoshuai) using DV cameras to document unauthorized, unofficial urban China; Jia Zhangke's 'Still Life' (2006, Venice Golden Lion) is the canonical Sixth Generation achievement.

The 'storyboard' — sequential drawings of a film's shots used to pre-visualize scenes before shooting — was pioneered at Disney in the 1930s and adopted for live-action by Alfred Hitchcock, who storyboarded entire films before a frame was shot; the 'Psycho' shower scene required 70 storyboard drawings for 50 seconds of screen time with 70 cuts.

The 'Cannes Film Market' (Marché du Film), held alongside the festival, is the world's largest film market — with over 12,000 industry professionals and 2,500 films screened in 2023; international co-production deals, streaming rights, and distribution agreements worth billions of euros are negotiated here, making it the primary global marketplace for independent film financing.

James Cameron spent 12 years developing the technology required to make 'Avatar' (2009) — including the 'Simulcam' system allowing actors on a performance capture stage to see a real-time rendering of their avatar interacting with the CGI environment; the film's $2.9 billion gross made it the highest-grossing film in history (surpassed only by its own sequel 'Avatar: The Way of Water' in 2022).

The 'Score,' as distinct from source music (music that originates within the film's world, like a radio playing) and non-diegetic underscore, creates cinema's emotional architecture; Max Steiner's score for 'King Kong' (1933) — the first major Hollywood film score — synchronized music to action with 'mickey-mousing' and established the conventions still used in action and adventure films.

The 'color correction' vs. 'color grading' distinction: color correction adjusts footage to a technical baseline (correcting exposure and white balance), while color grading creates an expressive 'look' — the teal-and-orange look (warming highlights, cooling shadows) became a dominant Hollywood aesthetic from 2005–2015, used in 'Michael Bay films,' 'Transformers,' and eventually parodied as a visual cliché.

The 'two-reeler' (20-minute films) was the dominant theatrical comedy format from 1912 to 1929; Mack Sennett's Keystone Studios produced slapstick comedies at an industrial pace (560 films in 8 years) using a permanent company of actors including Charlie Chaplin, Fatty Arbuckle, and Harold Lloyd; the Keystone Cops became the universal symbol of cinematic chaos.

The 'Film Noir Revival' ('neo-noir') of the 1970s–2000s — including Roman Polanski's 'Chinatown' (1974), Lawrence Kasdan's 'Body Heat' (1981), the Coen Brothers' 'Blood Simple' (1984), and 'LA Confidential' (1997) — reworked noir's moral ambiguity with contemporary social awareness; David Lynch's 'Blue Velvet' (1986) and 'Mulholland Drive' (2001) extended it into surrealism.

The 'Cannes Palme d'Or' — the festival's highest prize, established in 1955 (its golden palm design derived from the palm trees of Cannes) — has been awarded to 'The Tree of Life' (2011), '4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days' (2007), 'Parasite' (2019), and 'Titane' (2021, the second film by a woman to win in the festival's history); Francis Ford Coppola won the Palme twice ('The Conversation,' 1974; 'Apocalypse Now,' 1979).

The 'Hollywood foreign press association' (HFPA), founded by 88 international journalists in 1943 and responsible for the Golden Globe Awards, faced a major controversy in 2021 when the Los Angeles Times revealed it had no Black members among its 87 members, triggering a boycott by major studios and talent agencies that forced the organization to restructure its membership.

The 'Digital Projection revolution' — the conversion of movie theaters from 35mm film to digital projection beginning in the mid-2000s — was financially driven by studios seeking to eliminate the $1,500 cost of manufacturing and shipping each 35mm print (multiplied by thousands of theaters); by 2015, 98% of US cinema screens were digital, making 35mm projection a specialty service for film purists.

The Academy Award for Best Animated Feature was only established in 2002 (won by 'Shrek,' controversially beating 'Monsters, Inc.'); before that, animated films competed directly with live-action in the Best Picture category — 'Beauty and the Beast' (1991) was the first animated film nominated for Best Picture, a feat not repeated until 'Up' (2009).

text: The 'Cannes palme d'or rejection' is as famous as its winners: Michael Haneke's 'Cache' (2005) controversially won only Best Director; Jacques Rivette's 'Out 1' (1971, 12.5 hours long) was never entered; and Robert Bresson, arguably France's greatest director, never won the Palme despite four nominations — a reminder that film festival prizes reflect jury preferences as much as artistic merit.

The 'two-shot' in documentary — placing the interviewer and subject in the same frame — conveys the collaborative nature of the interview; Errol Morris pioneered the 'Interrotron' (1988), a device using half-silvered mirrors to allow subjects to look directly into the lens while appearing to maintain eye contact with the interviewer, creating an unprecedented sense of direct audience address in documentaries like 'The Fog of War' (2003).

The 'horror movie trailer' has developed its own grammar: the 'stinger' (abrupt loud sound cut to silence), the slow reveal of the monster, the fragmented editing that obscures narrative, and the dissonant musical motif; film sound designer and theorist Michel Chion argues that cinema's deepest fears are sonically triggered — the uncanny sound that precedes the image of dread.

Alfred Hitchcock's cameo appearances in his own films — a running joke from the 1920s — became so expected that by the 1960s audiences played 'spot the Hitchcock' games; his 1963 film 'The Birds' required his cameo early in the film so as not to distract viewers as the tension built; this self-referential quality made him one of cinema's first 'brand name' directors.

The 'DSLR revolution' in filmmaking was triggered when Canon's EOS 5D Mark II (2008) became the first consumer DSLR with full HD video recording; its large sensor produced a cinematic 'shallow depth of field' look previously achievable only with expensive cinema cameras; this democratized 'film look' video and enabled independent and documentary filmmakers to produce cinema-quality images for a fraction of previous costs.

The 'Hollywood Ten' — the 10 film industry professionals (including screenwriters Dalton Trumbo and Ring Lardner Jr.) who refused to cooperate with HUAC in 1947, citing their First Amendment rights, and were sentenced to prison for contempt of Congress — became symbols of artistic resistance to McCarthyism; their blacklisting devastated careers for over a decade.

The 'Mumblecore' movement in American independent cinema (mid-2000s), associated with directors Andrew Bujalski, Joe Swanberg, and the Duplass Brothers, made extremely low-budget films about post-college ennui using improvised dialogue, non-professional actors, and hand-held digital cameras; its aesthetics — intimate, underdramatic, naturalistic — influenced contemporary 'prestige television' acting styles.

Pedro Almodóvar — whose films celebrate female subjectivity, melodrama, sexuality, and Spain's transition from Francoism — won the Oscar for Best Foreign Film for 'All About My Mother' (1999) and 'Talk to Her' (2002); his late career film 'Pain and Glory' (2019) was seen as a self-portrait, and his debut English-language feature 'The Room Next Door' (2024) won the Golden Lion at Venice.

The 'zoom-in to reverse dolly' technique used in the opening of Stanley Kubrick's 'The Shining' (1980) — a helicopter shot tracking a car along mountain roads — was among the earliest feature film uses of a helicopter-mounted Steadicam (the 'Tyler helicopter mount'); Kubrick's team invented or adapted much of the camera technology used, including the first use of a zoom-on-a-zoom for the maze sequence.

Kathryn Bigelow became the first woman to win the Academy Award for Best Director for 'The Hurt Locker' (2009); at the ceremony she beat former husband James Cameron's 'Avatar' — the two films were the top-grossing and most-awarded of that Oscar season; despite the historic win, Bigelow is one of only three women (with Jane Campion and Chloe Zhao) to have won the Best Director Oscar.

text: Film preservation standards require maintaining multiple elements: the camera negative, an interpositive, an internegative, and a safety print; for color films, the three-strip 'separation masters' (separate black-and-white copies of each primary color record) provide archival stability independent of dye fade; the Library of Congress estimates over $4 billion would be needed to restore all at-risk films in US archives.

The 'experimental film' tradition — from Maya Deren's 'Meshes of the Afternoon' (1943) through Stan Brakhage's hand-painted films to Michael Snow's 'Wavelength' (1967, a 45-minute slow zoom across a loft) — constitutes a parallel cinema history largely invisible to mainstream audiences but profoundly influential on video art, installation art, and music video aesthetics.

The 'mockumentary' television format achieved its greatest popular success with the BBC's 'The Office' (2001–2003, created by Ricky Gervais and Stephen Merchant), remade in the US with even greater success (2005–2013, created by Greg Daniels), establishing 'single-camera comedy with talking heads' as the dominant form of American workplace comedy for two decades.

Martin Scorsese's 2019 New York Times opinion piece declaring Marvel films 'not cinema' — arguing they are closer to theme park rides than the medium of personal expression represented by Fellini, Cassavetes, and Bergman — triggered the most widely discussed debate about cinematic value in decades, with responses from filmmakers including Francis Ford Coppola, Pedro Almodóvar, and James Gunn.

The 'Pirated DVD market' in China, Southeast Asia, and Nigeria was, paradoxically, a powerful force for cinema education — millions encountered Bresson, Tarkovsky, and Wong Kar-wai on bootleg DVDs before legal streaming existed; Nollywood's direct-to-market VCD/DVD model also demonstrated that informal distribution systems can sustain national cinemas in the absence of formal theater infrastructure.

The 'Three-Act Structure' — the dominant model for Hollywood screenplay structure (Setup, Confrontation, Resolution), codified by Syd Field in 'Screenplay' (1979) — has been both the most taught and most challenged framework in film education; Blake Snyder's 'Save the Cat!' (2005) refined it to 15 'beats,' and its detractors argue it reduces cinema to a formula that privileges commercial predictability over artistic risk.

The history of film criticism includes its transformation from newspaper column to academic discipline to YouTube video essay; Pauline Kael (New Yorker, 1968–1991) and Roger Ebert (Chicago Sun-Times, 1967–2013) were the dominant popular critics of their era; Ebert's 1975 Pulitzer Prize for Criticism (the first awarded to a film critic) legitimized film as a serious critical subject in American journalism.

The 'video assist' system — a video tap mounted on the film camera allowing directors to view each take on a monitor immediately after shooting — was invented by Jerry Lewis (who used it on 'The Ladies Man,' 1961); before video assist, directors waited until dailies were processed the next day to see what they had shot, making video assist one of filmmaking's most significant quality-control innovations.

The '#OscarsSoWhite' hashtag, launched by April Reign in January 2016 after all 20 acting nominees were white for the second consecutive year, triggered the AMPAS's most significant membership reform — 928 new members were invited, doubling the pace of diversification, and by 2020 Black director Barry Jenkins had won Best Picture for 'Moonlight' (2016) and Chloé Zhao for 'Nomadland' (2020).

text: The Academy Award for Best International Feature Film (formerly Best Foreign Language Film), established in 1948, has been disproportionately dominated by European cinema; Italy has won the most (14 times), followed by France (12), and the Soviet Union/Russia (4); Japan has 4 wins (including 'Rashomon' honorary 1952 and 'Departures' 2008), while the first non-European non-Japanese winner was '2012 Amour' (Austria).

text: Robert Bresson's theory of 'cinematography' (as distinct from 'cinema') held that film should use non-professional 'models' rather than actors, suppress psychological expression, and strip away everything theatrical to achieve a spiritual spareness; his 13 features — including 'A Man Escaped' (1956), 'Pickpocket' (1959), and 'Au Hasard Balthazar' (1966, about a donkey) — are among cinema's most austere and revered works.

The 'GoPro revolution' — lightweight, rugged action cameras that mount to helmets, surfboards, and car hoods — brought subjective, visceral point-of-view cinematography into mainstream culture; their footage, originally used by extreme sports enthusiasts, became a new documentary language, influencing the visual style of war journalism, sports broadcasting, and narrative films seeking raw immediacy.

The 'French Impressionist' cinema of the 1920s (Germaine Dulac, Abel Gance, Marcel L'Herbier) used subjective camera techniques — superimpositions, soft focus, distorted lenses — to render inner psychological states; Dulac's 'The Seashell and the Clergyman' (1928) is often considered the first Surrealist film, predating Buñuel and Dalí's 'Un Chien Andalou' (1929).

Abel Gance's 'Napoleon' (1927) was the most technically ambitious silent film ever made — using three synchronized projectors to display a triptych wide image (a precursor to CinemaScope), handheld cameras strapped to horses and swinging pendulums, and a 5.5-hour runtime; its 1981 restoration with a live orchestra by Francis Ford Coppola introduced it to modern audiences.

The 'deep focus' cinematography that Orson Welles and Gregg Toland pioneered in 'Citizen Kane' (1941) required extraordinarily powerful lighting — 10,000-watt carbon arc lamps heating the set to temperatures that caused actors' contact lenses to warp; the technical difficulty of achieving truly deep focus meant it was rarely attempted again until anamorphic lenses improved in the 1960s.

The 'DCP' (Digital Cinema Package), the standard format for theatrical digital film distribution since 2005, uses JPEG2000 compression inside an MXF container at resolutions up to 4K (4096×2160); DCPs are delivered on hard drives or via satellite and require encrypted 'KDMs' (Key Delivery Messages) — essentially digital keys that allow projection only at authorized theaters during authorized windows.

The 'IMAX 70mm' format — 10 times the area of standard 35mm film — produces images of extraordinary resolution and detail; Christopher Nolan's 'Dunkirk' (2017) and 'Oppenheimer' (2023) were shot primarily on 65mm IMAX cameras; the distinctive IMAX aspect ratio (1.43:1) fills the full screen height, providing a dramatically different viewing experience from standard theatrical presentations.

The 'animation pipeline' at major studios like Pixar involves up to 27 distinct departments from story (2-year development) through modeling, rigging, shading, animation, effects, lighting, and final rendering; a single frame of 'Monsters University' (2013) required up to 100 hours to render, and the film's total rendering time was equivalent to running a single computer for 100 million hours.

The 'restoration' of 'Lawrence of Arabia' (1962) for its 1989 theatrical re-release — supervised by producer Robert A. Harris and director of photography Freddie Young — required tracking down original camera negative elements in vaults in London, New York, and Hong Kong, chemically restoring faded Technicolor dye layers, and reconstructing the 70mm six-track stereophonic mix from surviving magnetic elements.

Vilmos Zsigmond's cinematography for 'McCabe & Mrs. Miller' (1971, Robert Altman) used 'flashing' — briefly exposing unexposed film to a small amount of light before photography to reduce contrast and create a desaturated, weathered period look — a technique that influenced an entire generation of 1970s American cinematographers seeking alternatives to the high-contrast Technicolor aesthetic.

The 'Sprocket Damage' aesthetic — the look of super-8 film with visible frame lines and sprocket holes, degraded stock, light leaks, and grain — has been deliberately reproduced digitally as a marker of authenticity and nostalgia; the 'Filmic Pro' app and dozens of LUTs (Look-Up Tables) allow smartphone videographers to simulate the imperfections of 1970s amateur film cameras.

Agnès Varda's 'The Gleaners and I' (2000), shot on a lightweight digital camera she carried herself, pioneered the personal documentary essay film; Varda filmed herself filming, commented on the limitations of her aging body, and explored the ethical parallel between gleaners (who collect leftover crops after harvest) and documentary filmmakers who gather others' stories.

The 'Zoetrope' film studio founded by Francis Ford Coppola in 1969 was a genuine attempt to create an artist-centered alternative to the studio system; Apocalypse Now (1979) and One from the Heart (1982, shot entirely in-studio on a $27 million budget that nearly bankrupted Coppola) were its defining productions, demonstrating both the ambition and the financial risks of auteur-driven studio independence.

The 'Bollywood dance number' — an elaborately choreographed musical sequence inserted into a narrative film regardless of genre — derives from the tradition of Indian classical dance-drama and the influence of Hollywood musicals; A.R. Rahman, who composed for films including 'Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge' (1995) and 'Slumdog Millionaire' (2008), is the most successful composer in the tradition.

Saul Bass, the graphic designer who created title sequences for Hitchcock ('Vertigo,' 'Psycho,' 'North by Northwest'), Otto Preminger, and Martin Scorsese, elevated the film title sequence from functional information to art; his animated title sequence for 'Psycho' — jagged horizontal lines splitting the name — expressed the film's central theme of fragmented identity, influencing all subsequent title design.

The 'Palme d'Or refused' cases — Jean-Luc Godard refused the Grand Prix for 'Contempt' (1963) because he was unhappy with the print; Roberto Rossellini and Ingmar Bergman reportedly never submitted films to Cannes in protest of jury politics — demonstrate that major filmmakers have often viewed film festival prizes with ambivalence or contempt.

The 'French New Wave' directors' practice of shooting in Paris streets without permits, using available light and improvised schedules, was enabled by new lightweight 16mm cameras and fast film stocks (Ilford and Kodak's new emulsions allowed shooting in existing light); this practical liberalization of film production, combined with auteur ideology, created the template for all subsequent low-budget independent cinema.

The earliest known surviving film is Louis Aimé Augustin Le Prince's 'Roundhay Garden Scene' (1888), a 2.11-second clip shot in Leeds, England, predating the Lumière Brothers' first public screening by 7 years; Le Prince disappeared mysteriously in 1890, never able to claim his place in cinema history — one of the medium's most enduring mysteries.

The 'cinematheque' tradition — public archives and screening venues dedicated to film history — was pioneered by Henri Langlois, who co-founded the Cinémathèque Française in Paris in 1936 and almost single-handedly saved thousands of films from destruction; Langlois's illegal screeninings of prohibited German films during the Nazi occupation formed the cinematic education of Godard, Truffaut, and the entire French New Wave.

The 'underwater cinematography' challenge was solved for major productions beginning with James Cameron's 'The Abyss' (1989) and for natural history with the BBC's 'Blue Planet' (2001); 'The Blue Planet II' (2017) used custom-built submersibles at depths of 1,000 meters, 4K ultra-high definition cameras, and specially designed lighting rigs that had no precedent in marine documentary production.

The 'Godfather' cinematographer Gordon Willis, known as 'The Prince of Darkness,' deliberately underexposed faces and placed key light sources below the frame in 'The Godfather' (1972), violating every rule of conventional film lighting; Paramount was alarmed and almost demanded reshoots before early screenings proved his aesthetic to be among the most influential in Hollywood history.

The 'Dogme 95' rule forbidding non-diegetic music (sound not produced within the film's world) forced directors to develop alternative emotional strategies; Lars von Trier's 'The Idiots' (1998) used improv scenes and the ambient sounds of locations; Thomas Vinterberg acknowledged that 'Festen' (1998) violated the Vow of Chastity in several ways but that Dogme's value was in forcing creative constraint.

The 'Phantom camera' — ultra-high-speed digital cameras capable of shooting at up to 1,000,000 frames per second (compared to cinema's standard 24 fps) — has transformed both scientific visualization and commercial filmmaking; used in BBC's 'Planet Earth II' (2016) to capture hummingbird wing beats and in commercials to create hyper-slow-motion images, it reveals a visual world otherwise imperceptible to the human eye.

The 'Aaton' 16mm camera, designed by Jean-Pierre Beauviala in Grenoble in the 1970s and dubbed 'the cat on your shoulder' for its ergonomic design, enabled a new generation of documentary filmmakers to shoot in extreme conditions; its successor, the Aaton XTR, became the standard camera for ethnographic and observational documentary work for three decades.

The 'Blaxploitation' film 'Shaft' (1971), directed by Gordon Parks with an Isaac Hayes score, was so commercially successful that it saved MGM from bankruptcy; this economic power of Black-audience cinema — long dismissed by Hollywood — was a direct precursor to the 1990s 'New Black Cinema' of Spike Lee, John Singleton ('Boyz n the Hood,' 1991), and Julie Dash.

The 'sneak preview' or 'test screening' — showing a rough cut to sample audiences before release to gauge reactions — became standard Hollywood practice after the 1979 release of 'Heaven's Gate' bypassed previews and became the film that destroyed United Artists; studios now routinely spend $30,000–$100,000 per screening on focus groups and audience tracking surveys.

Spike Lee's 'Do the Right Thing' (1989), shot by Ernest Dickerson with saturated 'hot' colors to reflect the literal and social heat of a Brooklyn summer day, deliberately violated the 180-degree rule to create visual disorientation; its ending — in which violence seems equally attributable to police and rioters — was condemned by critics including Joe Klein before release as potentially 'inciting riots,' a charge that has been retrospectively examined in light of Black Lives Matter.

The 'tracking shot' or 'dolly shot' — a camera moving physically through space on wheels or a crane — creates a distinctly different temporal experience from cutting; Stanley Kubrick's 'The Shining' Steadicam tracks following Danny on his tricycle, Scorsese's Copacabana entrance in 'Goodfellas,' and Welles's opening crane shot in 'Touch of Evil' (1958, a 3.5-minute uninterrupted take) are among cinema's most technically admired.

The 'casting couch' — the exploitation of aspiring actors by producers and directors — became a systemic industry scandal with the #MeToo movement's exposure of Harvey Weinstein in October 2017; the resulting 'Time's Up' campaign, formation of the Commission on Sexual Harassment and Advancing Equality, and industry reckoning fundamentally altered power dynamics in Hollywood production.

The 'Film Forum' in New York City (founded 1970), the Nuart in Los Angeles (1947), and the ICA Cinema in London represent a global network of independent cinemas dedicated to repertory programming — showing classic, experimental, and foreign films that would not receive mainstream theatrical distribution; their programming function is distinct from archives and cinematheques, providing a public exhibition venue for film culture.

The 'Zapruder film' — 26 seconds of 8mm home movie footage taken by Abraham Zapruder on November 22, 1963, capturing the assassination of President Kennedy — is the most analyzed amateur footage in history; its contested interpretation (the 'back and to the left' head movement was central to debates about the number of shooters) demonstrated how film evidence could become a site of political and forensic contest.

The 'Japanese studio Nikkatsu,' founded in 1912 (Japan's oldest film studio), survived periods of military censorship, American occupation, and financial crisis by pivoting in 1971 to 'Roman Porno' (soft-core erotic films with strict rules about nudity frequency but near-total creative freedom for directors); this policy inadvertently produced a decade of creative cinema that launched directors including Masaru Konuma and Noboru Tanaka.

The 'Film negative' as commodity was not universally considered valuable for preservation: studios discarded, donated, or lost thousands of nitrate negatives between the 1950s and 1970s; the Fox vault fire of 1937, the Universal vault fire of 2008 (which destroyed 500,000 master recordings), and numerous other accidents have permanently eliminated portions of cinema history that no amount of restoration can recover.

The 'super-8 film' format, introduced by Kodak in 1965, democratized amateur filmmaking for a generation; the home-movie aesthetic it created — grainy, slightly shaky, with warm colors and lens flares — became a powerful signifier of memory and nostalgia exploited by directors from Steven Spielberg to J.J. Abrams in 'Super 8' (2011), a film explicitly about childhood filmmaking in the super-8 era.

The 'Surrealist photography' of Man Ray — who invented the 'Rayograph' (photogram made without a camera by placing objects on photosensitive paper) and the 'Solarization' technique (briefly exposing a developing print to light) — established photography as a medium for irrational, dreamlike imagery rather than documentary record, influencing fashion photography, advertising, and fine art to the present day.

The 'Dogme 95' movement's influence extended beyond its 35 official certified films (1998–2005); its emphasis on digital, handheld, unlit filmmaking became the default aesthetic for reality television, which launched globally in the late 1990s; 'The Real World' (MTV, 1992), 'Big Brother' (1999), and 'Survivor' (2000) all adopted cinema vérité aesthetics that Dogme had theorized.

The 'Paris, Texas' (1984, Wim Wenders, cinematography Robby Müller) use of the American Southwest landscape as a visual correlative for emotional desolation — shot using the wide open spaces of Texas and the Mojave Desert to dwarf characters and suggest spiritual emptiness — established a 'road movie' visual grammar that influenced Terrence Malick, David Lynch, and an entire lineage of American art cinema.

The 'Hollywood system' of 'vertical integration' — studios owning production, distribution, and exhibition (theaters) — was declared illegal by the US Supreme Court in 'United States v. Paramount Pictures' (1948), forcing studios to divest theater chains; this 'Paramount Decree' is considered the legal foundation of the modern independent film industry, as studios could no longer guarantee their films' exhibition.

The 'Kinetoscope,' Thomas Edison's 1891 peephole viewing device — in which a single viewer watched a short film loop through a magnifying eyepiece — was deliberately designed to prevent group viewing and maximize per-view revenue; the Lumière Brothers' projection innovation (allowing mass audiences) was partly a response to Edison's monopolistic approach, demonstrating how business decisions shape technology.

The 'Spaghetti Western' composer Ennio Morricone's technique of using unusual instruments — electric guitar, ocarina, whistle, gunshots, and the human voice as melody rather than harmony — in 'The Good, the Bad and the Ugly' (1966) created a film music vocabulary simultaneously avant-garde and commercially irresistible; Morricone reportedly composed over 500 film scores, making him the most prolific significant film composer in history.

The 'Cinematograph' patent filed by the Lumière Brothers in February 1895 described a device that was simultaneously camera, projector, and printing machine — a combined apparatus serving all three functions; this elegant simplicity contrasted with Edison's separate Kinetograph (camera) and Kinetoscope (viewer), and enabled the Lumières to shoot, process, and project their films with minimal equipment.

Béla Tarr's 'Sátántangó' (1994) — shot over several years in actual Hungarian village locations including real mud, real weather, and real decay — used 8-minute average shot lengths to create a near-physical experience of rural poverty and futility; Tarr collaborated with writer László Krasznahorkai on the film (adapted from his novel), a partnership that produced six films spanning three decades.

The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences' 'Scientific and Technical Awards' — the 'Scientific Oscars' — honor breakthrough technologies that have transformed filmmaking; past winners include the development of computer-generated imagery, digital audio mixing, digital intermediate processing, and in 2020 the contributions of researchers to volumetric performance capture that enabled 'The Mandalorian's' virtual production system.

text: The 'virtual production' LED stage pioneered in 'The Mandalorian' (2019, ILM's 'StageCraft' technology) allows actors to perform within a 270-degree LED wall displaying real-time photorealistic environments; unlike traditional green screen, the LED background responds to camera angle and provides accurate light on the actors' faces, fundamentally changing the economics of location filmmaking.

The 'Dolby Atmos' sound system (2012), which places sounds in a three-dimensional space including height channels through up to 64 speakers, represents the most significant advance in theatrical film sound since Dolby Stereo (1977); it was first used in 'Brave' (Pixar, 2012) and has since been adopted for home theaters and headphone listening, enabling 'spatial audio' that approximates surround sound on standard earbuds.

Claude Lanzmann's 'Shoah' (1985) — a 9.5-hour documentary on the Holocaust using no archival footage, only contemporary interviews with survivors, perpetrators, and bystanders — represents the most radical position in documentary ethics: that the Holocaust cannot be represented by historical images but only by living testimony; Lanzmann's opposition to Steven Spielberg's 'Schindler's List' (1993) sparked one of cinema's deepest ethical debates.

The 'Cinéma du look' French style of the 1980s (Luc Besson's 'Subway,' 1985; Jean-Jacques Beineix's 'Diva,' 1981; Leos Carax's 'Boy Meets Girl,' 1984) prioritized visual style, strong primary colors, and stylized set design over social realism; simultaneously celebrated as a new French aesthetic and criticized as 'postcard cinema,' it influenced music video aesthetics and commercial filmmaking worldwide.

The 'Netflix effect' on global cinema — where the platform's algorithm, based on viewing data from 238 million subscribers, influences what films get made, how they are marketed, and what constitutes 'quality' — represents a fundamental shift from critic-driven to data-driven film culture; Netflix's practice of not releasing box-office numbers breaks the traditional transparency of theatrical exhibition.

The 'Persistence of vision' theory — the long-held belief that cinema creates the illusion of motion because the human eye retains images briefly after they disappear — has been partially replaced by 'phi phenomenon' and 'beta movement' as more accurate neurological explanations; cinema actually exploits multiple neurological mechanisms including stroboscopic effect, visual masking, and the brain's desire to complete incomplete patterns.

The 'road movie' genre — defined by journey as both literal and metaphysical subject — has produced national variants reflecting each country's relationship to landscape and mobility: American (Easy Rider, Thelma & Louise), German (Paris, Texas; Kings of the Road by Wim Wenders), Iranian (Kiarostami's Koker trilogy), and Indian (Dil Dhadakne Do); all use movement through space as a metaphor for psychological and social change.

The Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers (SMPTE), founded in 1916, has standardized every technical aspect of film and television including frame rates (24fps film, 25fps PAL, 29.97fps NTSC), color spaces, resolution standards, and timecode; its standards enable a film shot in Los Angeles on an ARRI ALEXA to be edited in London and projected in Tokyo without technical incompatibility.

The 'Hays Code's' prohibition on depicting successful crime without punishment paradoxically intensified pre-Code Hollywood's fascination with gangsters; films like 'The Public Enemy' (1931) and 'Scarface' (1932) made gangsters glamorous anti-heroes before censors clamped down; Francis Ford Coppola's 'The Godfather' (1972) drew on this tradition to create American cinema's most enduring mythological figure.

The 'close-up' in cinema — extreme proximity to a face or object — was introduced in film grammar by D.W. Griffith but theorized by Soviet filmmaker Béla Balázs (1924) as cinema's unique revelation of the human face; Balázs argued that the close-up creates 'physiognomy' — expressing inner psychological life through minute muscular movement imperceptible to theater audiences — as cinema's distinct contribution to performance art.

Film score pioneer Max Steiner's 240-minute score for 'Gone with the Wind' (1939) — using over 50 themes for characters and situations — remains the longest Hollywood score ever written, requiring four months of orchestration and 70 hours of music (though edited down significantly); it set the standard for the 'classical Hollywood score' style that defined film music for 40 years.

The 'New Hollywood's' lasting gift was an expansion of cinematic subject matter: before 1967, homosexuality, drug use, graphic violence, miscegenation, and moral ambiguity were banned by the Hays Code; within five years all appeared in mainstream Hollywood films; the films from this period — 'Easy Rider,' 'Midnight Cowboy' (1969, the only X-rated Best Picture winner), 'The French Connection' — permanently changed what American audiences expect from cinema.

The 'black and white' choice in contemporary filmmaking — used by directors including Steven Spielberg in 'Schindler's List' (1993), Alfonso Cuarón in 'Roma' (2018), and Kenneth Branagh in 'Belfast' (2021) — is rarely technological necessity but a deliberate aesthetic statement, typically associated with historical memory, documentary authenticity, or artistic seriousness that distinguishes films from commercial entertainment.

The 'production design' department — responsible for all visual elements of a film's physical world including sets, props, costumes, and color palette — operates through the production designer (formerly 'art director') who translates the director's vision into a coherent physical world; William Cameron Menzies, credited as 'Production Designer' on 'Gone with the Wind' (1939), created the job title and its scope.

The 'Ektachrome' color reversal film that NASA used to photograph every Apollo mission has a distinctive warm, high-saturation look that became the visual signature of 1960s–70s American documentary photography; Kodak discontinued Ektachrome in 2012 and then revived it in 2018 in response to analog photography's cultural revival, demonstrating nostalgia's economic power.

The 'Giallo' film — an Italian genre of lurid, stylistically excessive horror-mystery films (named after the yellow covers of pulp crime novels) pioneered by Mario Bava and Dario Argento in the 1960s–80s — influenced virtually all subsequent horror aesthetics through its elaborate kill sequences, POV shots, expressionist color, and prog-rock scores; Argento's 'Suspiria' (1977) and 'Deep Red' (1975) are canonical examples.

The Sundance Institute's January film festival in Park City, Utah has grown from a small regional showcase (1985) to the world's most important platform for independent film; films including 'sex, lies, and videotape' (1989), 'Reservoir Dogs' (1992), 'Pulp Fiction' (1994 as buyer's market), 'Little Miss Sunshine' (2006), and 'Beasts of the Southern Wild' (2012) all launched at Sundance.

The 'Nouvelle Vague Rive Gauche' (Left Bank) — a less celebrated but equally radical strand of French New Wave associated with Alain Resnais ('Hiroshima Mon Amour,' 1959), Agnes Varda ('Cleo from 5 to 7,' 1962), and Chris Marker ('La Jetée,' 1962) — was more politically engaged, more influenced by literary modernism, and less interested in genre than the Cahiers-connected New Wave.

The 'Film rating system' varies dramatically internationally: Germany's FSK uses detailed age classifications and prohibits children being brought to certain screenings; Japan's Eirin has separate tracks for general, adult, and R-18 content; while Australia's Classification Board can ban films entirely as 'RC' (Refused Classification) — 'A Serbian Film' (2010) was banned in Australia, Norway, and several other countries.

Patricio Guzmán's 'The Battle of Chile' (1975–1979) — a three-part documentary on Allende's overthrow and Pinochet's coup, shot clandestinely and smuggled out of Chile in diplomatic pouches — is considered the most important Latin American political documentary; the footage, shot by Jorge Müller Silva (who disappeared after the coup), was cut in Cuba over four years, demonstrating how documentary filmmaking can become a form of historical witness under authoritarianism.

The 'musical' film genre — in which characters spontaneously sing and dance as emotional expression — was Hollywood's dominant form from the 1930s through the 1960s; the genre's perceived artificiality led to its near-extinction in the 1980s–90s, before revivals including 'Moulin Rouge!' (2001), 'Chicago' (2002), 'La La Land' (2016), and animated features sustained its commercial viability.

The 'Academy ratio' (1.37:1) was established by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in 1932 as the standard aspect ratio following the introduction of sound (which required space for the optical soundtrack, narrowing the frame); until CinemaScope in 1953, virtually all Hollywood films were shot in this almost square ratio, which is now associated with the look of classic Hollywood and is occasionally revived for aesthetic effect.

text: The 'Cannes Film Festival's' original 1939 edition was cancelled after opening day because of Germany's invasion of Poland; it resumed in 1946 with a jury that included writers Jean Cocteau and Aldous Huxley; the 1960 festival introduced the Palme d'Or design by Lucienne Lazon — a gold palm leaf on a black background — that remains cinema's most prestigious single trophy.

The 'Oscars envelope error' at the 89th Academy Awards (2017) — when the wrong Best Picture winner ('La La Land') was announced before the actual winner ('Moonlight') was revealed — was caused by PricewaterhouseCoopers accountant Brian Cullinan tweeting a backstage photo and handing the wrong envelope to presenters Faye Dunaway and Warren Beatty; it remains the most widely viewed live mistake in television history.
