text: The Paramount Decree of 1948 (United States v. Paramount Pictures, Inc.) forced the major studios to divest their theater chains, breaking the vertical integration that had given them guaranteed distribution of their films; historians consider this Supreme Court antitrust decision as ending the Golden Age studio system and enabling independent film production to flourish.

The persistence of vision theory — that cinema works by exploiting the eye's tendency to retain images for a fraction of a second, creating the illusion of motion from still frames — was the standard explanation of cinema for over a century; it was largely debunked in the 1970s and replaced by the 'phi phenomenon' (apparent motion) as the actual perceptual mechanism enabling moving images.

The 'Kuleshov Effect,' demonstrated by Soviet filmmaker Lev Kuleshov in the early 1920s, showed that the same close-up of an actor's neutral face is perceived as expressing hunger, grief, or desire depending on what image follows it in the edit — establishing that meaning in cinema is created between shots rather than within them, the foundational principle of film editing.

D.W. Griffith's 'The Birth of a Nation' (1915) simultaneously established many foundational techniques of film grammar (cross-cutting, close-ups, tracking shots, iris effects) and presented virulent KKK propaganda as historical fact, inspiring a resurgence of Klan membership; it remains cinema's most morally controversial canonical film, raising permanent questions about the separation of aesthetic achievement from ideology.

The iris shot — a circular mask that opens or closes around a subject within the frame — was used extensively in silent cinema (particularly by D.W. Griffith) as a punctuation mark to focus attention on details or signal narrative transitions; it virtually disappeared after the introduction of sound and was revived as a nostalgic quotation by directors including Wes Anderson.

The 'reaction shot' — cutting from an action to a watching character's response — is one of cinema's most fundamental emotional tools; Alfred Hitchcock distinguished between 'suspense' (showing both the bomb under the table and characters talking above it) and 'surprise' (showing the explosion without warning), arguing that reaction shots were the mechanism by which audiences could experience sustained emotional engagement.

Vilém Flusser's 'Towards a Philosophy of Photography' (1983) argued that photographs are not windows onto reality but outputs of a 'technical apparatus' programmed to produce certain kinds of images; his concept that photographers are 'functionaries' of the camera program — their creativity constrained by the camera's design — anticipated debates about algorithmic image-making by 30 years.

Susan Sontag's 'On Photography' (1977), which argued that photographic images create a 'chronic voyeuristic relation to the world' and that photography diminishes experience by substituting representation for reality, remains the most widely read work of photographic theory; her later 'Regarding the Pain of Others' (2003) revised some of these positions by acknowledging photography's capacity to generate genuine moral witness.

Roland Barthes's 'Camera Lucida' (1980), written after his mother's death and structured around a photograph of her as a child, introduced the concepts of 'studium' (cultural, learned interest in an image) and 'punctum' (the personal, wounding detail that pierces the viewer unexpectedly); these terms have become fundamental to photography theory and art criticism.

The photographic index — the idea that a photograph has a physical causal connection to its subject (light reflected from the object literally exposed the film) — is fundamental to photography's truth claims; digital photography, which converts light into binary code with no chemical trace of the original, has technically severed this indexical link, raising unresolved questions about digital photography's epistemic status.

The 'Photo-Secession' movement founded by Alfred Stieglitz in 1902 published 'Camera Work' magazine (1903–1917), which printed photographs on platinum paper using hand-printing techniques with production values matching fine art books; its 50 issues, each featuring work by Stieglitz, Alvin Langdon Coburn, Edward Steichen, and others, are among the most collectible photography publications.

The 'concerned photography' movement — a term coined by Cornell Capa (Robert Capa's brother) for socially engaged humanist photography — was embodied by Magnum photographers including W. Eugene Smith, whose 1971–1972 photographs of mercury poisoning victims in Minamata, Japan, contributed to both legal accountability and the global environmental movement.

Nick Ut's 'Napalm Girl' (1972) — showing nine-year-old Kim Phuc fleeing a napalm attack in Vietnam — won the Pulitzer Prize and World Press Photo of the Year and is credited with turning American public opinion against the Vietnam War; in 2016 Facebook briefly removed the image as a violation of its nudity policy before reversing after worldwide protests.

Eddie Adams's photograph of South Vietnamese National Police Chief Nguyễn Ngọc Loan executing a Viet Cong prisoner (1968) won the Pulitzer Prize and became one of the most controversial war photographs ever taken; Adams later expressed regret, writing 'still photographs are the most powerful weapon in the world' while also acknowledging the image's failure to convey the full context of the moment.

Kevin Carter's 1993 photograph of a vulture watching a starving Sudanese child — which won the 1994 Pulitzer Prize for Feature Photography — generated enormous controversy about photojournalistic ethics; Carter committed suicide three months after receiving the prize, leaving a note that described being haunted by the images of famine, war, and murder he had photographed.

The World Press Photo contest, established in 1955 and headquartered in Amsterdam, annually receives entries from over 4,000 photographers in 130 countries; it is the most prestigious annual award in photojournalism, and its annual book and touring exhibition define the visual record of world events for millions of viewers who follow no individual photographer.

The 'death of photojournalism' narrative has recurred since the 1980s — first when editors reduced photo budgets, then when digital cameras destroyed the film processing labs that housed photo agencies, then when social media gave everyone a camera; each predicted death has instead produced adaptation, with photojournalists increasingly using multimedia, video, and social media to distribute work outside traditional editorial channels.

The Getty Images library, assembled through acquisitions including The Image Bank (1997), Tony Stone Images (1997), and Corbis (2016, visual licensing business), now controls over 477 million images — the largest commercial photograph archive in history; its licensing model and market dominance have been criticized for suppressing photography fees and concentrating image rights.

Sebastião Salgado's 'Genesis' project (2013) — eight years photographing pristine ecosystems and indigenous peoples across five continents on large-format film — was simultaneously the most ambitious nature photography project ever undertaken and a deliberate argument for returning to analog photography's tonal richness as a counter to digital photography's dominance.

James Nachtwey, the most decorated war photographer alive, has covered conflicts from Northern Ireland to Sarajevo to Rwanda and documented the AIDS crisis in Africa; he is one of the few photojournalists to have a major documentary made about his work — 'War Photographer' (2001, directed by Christian Frei) received an Academy Award nomination for Best Documentary Feature.

The 'decisive moment' in digital photography has been fundamentally altered by burst shooting — the ability to fire 30 or more frames per second — which allows photographers to select the perfect millisecond after the fact rather than anticipating it; critics argue this has eliminated the skill and intention that made Cartier-Bresson's concept meaningful as a photographic philosophy.

The RAW image format, which records unprocessed sensor data rather than processing it in-camera to JPEG, gives photographers complete post-processing control but creates files 5–6 times larger than JPEGs; the format's creation by camera manufacturers using proprietary codecs has led to long-term archival concerns — obsolete RAW formats from cameras discontinued in the 1990s are now unreadable on modern software.

The 'decisive moment' essay has been misattributed in its English title; Cartier-Bresson was quoting the 17th-century Cardinal de Retz ('There is nothing in this world that does not have a decisive moment') and applying the concept to photography; the misattribution created the false impression that Cartier-Bresson invented rather than borrowed and applied the philosophical concept.

The International Center of Photography (ICP) in New York, founded by Cornell Capa in 1974, was the first museum in the United States dedicated exclusively to photography; its school, which trained thousands of photographers, and its collection of over 200,000 photographs make it the world's leading institution for photographic education and exhibition.

The Aperture Foundation, established in 1952 by Minor White, Ansel Adams, Dorothea Lange, and others as an alternative to commercial photography magazines, published the 'Aperture' quarterly — the most influential photography magazine in American history — as well as hundreds of photography books that established the medium's canon in the second half of the 20th century.

The first photograph taken from a drone (technically a kite-borne camera) was made by meteorologist Arthur Batut in 1888 over the French town of Labruguière; modern consumer drones equipped with high-resolution cameras have completely democratized aerial photography, previously available only to those who could afford aircraft or helicopters.

source.name: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

text: The Platinum print, using platinum salts rather than silver to produce photographic images, has extraordinary archival permanence — surviving unchanged for over 200 years under normal storage conditions, compared to silver prints which can deteriorate within decades; contemporary fine art photographers including Irving Penn insisted on platinum printing for its tonal richness and longevity.

The cyanotype process, invented by Sir John Herschel in 1842, uses iron salts to produce distinctive Prussian blue photographs; botanist Anna Atkins used cyanotypes to create 'Photographs of British Algae: Cyanotype Impressions' (1843), which is widely considered the first photographically illustrated book ever published.

The tintype (ferrotype), introduced in 1856, produced inexpensive photographs on thin iron sheets that were nearly indestructible compared to glass and paper; tintype photographers could set up portable studios anywhere — at fairs, carnivals, or on battlefields — making them the dominant popular photography format in America from the Civil War through the 1890s.

The ambrotype, a positive photograph made on glass using the collodion process backed with dark material, was patented by James Ambrose Cutting in 1854; it was cheaper than a daguerreotype but less durable, and was largely replaced by the tintype and albumen print within a decade — demonstrating how quickly photographic formats can become obsolete.

Hiroshi Sugimoto's 'Theaters' series (1976–present) exposes film for the entire duration of a movie screening — the resulting single image shows the screen as a glowing rectangle of pure white light surrounded by empty theater seats, the entire film compressed into a single exposure; the series asks whether a photograph can contain time.

Andreas Gursky's 'Rhein II' (1999) — a digitally manipulated photograph of the Rhine River reduced to horizontal bands of gray and green — sold at Christie's in 2011 for $4.3 million, setting the record for the most expensive photograph ever sold at auction at the time; its price reflected both Gursky's reputation and debates about photography's relationship to painting.

Cindy Sherman's 'Untitled Film Stills' series (1977–1980) — 69 black-and-white photographs in which Sherman poses as female archetypes from B-movies without replicating any actual film — critiqued how cinema constructs femininity; the complete series was acquired by the Museum of Modern Art in 1995 for $1 million, then the highest price paid for a photography series.

Richard Prince's 'Cowboys' series (1983–1992) — large-format re-photographs of Marlboro cigarette advertisements cropped to remove branding — raised fundamental questions about authorship, copyright, and originality in photography; his re-photography practice, along with Sherrie Levine's re-photographs of Walker Evans, defined 'appropriation art' as a movement.

Nan Goldin's 'The Ballad of Sexual Dependency' — begun as a slideshow in 1979 and published as a book in 1986 — documented her social circle of lovers, friends, and drag queens through intimate, snapshot-style color photographs that portrayed sexuality, drug use, and domestic violence without judgment; it established confessional photography as a legitimate art form.

Wolfgang Tillmans, winner of the Turner Prize in 2000 — the first photographer and first non-British artist to receive the award — prints photographs in a wide range of scales from wallet-sized to room-filling and pins them directly to gallery walls without frames, challenging museum conventions about how photographs should be displayed.

Sally Mann's 'Immediate Family' (1992) — photographs of her three children in rural Virginia, sometimes showing them injured, naked, or in distressing situations — was the most controversial photography book of its decade; the debate about whether the images were art or exploitation established lasting precedents about children's rights and artistic freedom in photography.

Stephen Shore's 'Uncommon Places' (1982) — 8×10 large-format color photographs of ordinary American roadside landscapes — redefined 'serious' photography by treating banal subjects (parking lots, motel rooms, diners) with the formal rigor previously reserved for landscapes and portraits, directly influencing a generation of photographers including William Eggleston.

William Eggleston's 1976 exhibition at MoMA — the first solo exhibition of color photography at the museum — was initially dismissed by critics as 'snapshots of boring subjects,' but is now considered the exhibition that legitimized color photography as a fine art medium; his photograph 'Untitled (Greenwood, Mississippi)' (1973), showing a red ceiling, is one of the most reproduced art photographs.

The 'New Topographics' exhibition at George Eastman House (1975) — featuring Robert Adams, Lewis Baltz, Bernd and Hilla Becher, and others — presented deadpan photographs of industrial landscapes and suburban sprawl as aesthetic subjects; it established the documentary tradition of photographing human alteration of the natural environment that culminated in New Topographics-influenced work by Edward Burtynsky and others.

Edward Burtynsky's large-format photographs of oil refineries, ship-breaking yards, and mining operations in 'Manufactured Landscapes' (2006, accompanied by Jennifer Baichwal's documentary film) made industrial pollution aesthetically sublime — creating images beautiful enough to hang in galleries that also document environmental catastrophe, creating deliberate moral tension for viewers.

The Bechers, Bernd and Hilla — whose systematic typological photographs of industrial structures (water towers, coal bunkers, blast furnaces) influenced an entire generation of German photographers called the 'Düsseldorf School' — taught photography at the Düsseldorf Art Academy for 20 years; their students including Andreas Gursky, Thomas Struth, and Thomas Ruff became among the most commercially successful art photographers.

The 'decisive moment' in sports photography — capturing peak athletic action — was transformed by autofocus technology; the Canon EOS-1 (1989) was the first SLR with reliable phase-detection autofocus, enabling photographers to track moving subjects; modern sports cameras like the Canon EOS R3 use eye-tracking AI to lock focus on athletes' eyes at 30 frames per second.

Fashion photography originated in Paris with Baron Adolf de Meyer's idealized soft-focus portraits for 'Vogue' (1913–1921); Edward Steichen transformed fashion photography into an art form with his dynamic compositions for 'Vanity Fair' and 'Vogue' in the 1920s; Richard Avedon later stripped away glamour to reveal the artifice of fashion imagery itself.

Irving Penn's minimalist approach to fashion and portrait photography — placing subjects against plain white or gray seamless backgrounds, eliminating environmental context — was revolutionary when introduced at 'Vogue' in the 1940s; his 'Small Trades' series (1950–1951), photographing workers in their work clothes against the same neutral backgrounds, applied fashion photography's visual rigor to working people.

Helmut Newton's provocative fashion photographs for 'Vogue' and 'French Vogue' in the 1970s–1990s — featuring powerful, often naked women in dominance scenarios — were simultaneously celebrated as feminist (showing women as sexually powerful agents) and condemned as objectifying; Newton's work permanently complicated the relationship between fashion, eroticism, and gender power in commercial photography.

Herb Ritts's clean, high-contrast black-and-white celebrity and fashion photographs — influenced by the sculptural quality of classical Greek statuary — defined the visual language of 1980s Hollywood glamour; his photograph of a Versace model on a Harley-Davidson became one of the most reproduced fashion images of the decade.

The 1888 'Kodak Moment' advertising slogan — later refined to 'You press the button, we do the rest' — was arguably the first consumer photography marketing campaign; Kodak's subsequent 'Memories' and 'Share Moments, Share Life' campaigns established photography's cultural identity as primarily a memory preservation technology rather than an art form.

Instagram, launched in October 2010 and acquired by Facebook for $1 billion in 2012, transformed photography distribution more fundamentally than any technology since the printing press — enabling anyone to publish images to a global audience instantly and creating new genres including 'foodie photography,' 'selfie culture,' and 'influencer aesthetics' that did not exist before.

The selfie was named 'Word of the Year' by Oxford Dictionaries in 2013, having increased in usage by 17,000% in the preceding year; the selfie stick was subsequently named by Time magazine as one of the 25 best inventions of 2014; selfie culture's impact on photography ranges from face-tuning app distortions of body image to formal art practice by photographers including Cindy Sherman.

The Flickr photography platform, launched in 2004, was the first major social photography sharing site; at its peak (2008) it hosted over 4 billion images and was cited by academics as evidence that 'photography has become the world's dominant language'; its decline after Yahoo's acquisition and Instagram's rise illustrates how platform dependence endangers photographic archives.

Night photography was essentially impossible before fast panchromatic films in the 1920s; Brassaï's 'Paris by Night' (1933) — the first major book of night photography — used available gaslight, neon, and streetlamps to document Montmartre's nocturnal underground; his technical challenge of 20–30 minute exposures while hand-holding a camera produced images unlike anything previously seen.

High-speed photography, pioneered by Harold Edgerton at MIT using stroboscopic flash units he invented in the 1930s, captured images of events invisible to the human eye — a bullet piercing an apple, a drop of milk forming a coronet — and was used by the US military during WWII to document nuclear tests and ballistics; his milk drop photographs became iconic images of 20th-century science photography.

Macro photography, capturing subjects at life-size (1:1) magnification or greater, requires specialized optical designs because standard lenses cannot focus close enough; the genre reveals worlds invisible to the naked eye — pollen structure, insect eyes, water droplets on leaves — and has been practiced since the 1880s using bellows and extension tubes long before dedicated macro lenses existed.

Infrared photography, which records near-infrared light invisible to human eyes, produces distinctive images in which foliage appears white (due to strong infrared reflection from chlorophyll), skies turn dark, and skin glows ethereally; Kodak manufactured infrared film from 1931, and it was used in aerial reconnaissance because infrared light penetrates atmospheric haze better than visible light.

Ultraviolet (UV) fluorescence photography — illuminating subjects with UV light to capture fluorescent emissions invisible in normal light — has revealed hidden details in paintings, documents, minerals, and biological specimens; the technique was pioneered by Robert Wood in 1903 and is now standard in art conservation, forensic investigation, and dermatology.

X-ray photography, discovered accidentally by Wilhelm Röntgen in 1895 when he photographed his wife Bertha's hand (showing her ring and the bones beneath), was immediately applied medically within weeks of the discovery; Röntgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 for his discovery and is considered the originator of medical imaging.

Photogrammetry — the science of extracting three-dimensional measurements from photographs — was first described by François Arago in 1840 (the same year he announced the daguerreotype) and is now fundamental to architecture, archaeology, and topographic mapping; modern Structure from Motion (SfM) software can create accurate 3D models of objects and environments from smartphone photographs.

The 'Earthrise' photograph taken by astronaut William Anders during Apollo 8 on December 24, 1968 — showing the Earth rising over the lunar horizon in color for the first time — is considered by many environmental historians to have catalyzed the environmental movement and led directly to the first Earth Day (April 22, 1970); it has been called 'the most influential environmental photograph ever taken.'

The 'Blue Marble' photograph (AS17-148-22727), taken by the Apollo 17 crew on December 7, 1972, is believed to be the most widely reproduced photograph in history; unlike 'Earthrise,' which shows Earth partially, 'Blue Marble' shows the full disk of Earth in sunlight — an image so emotionally powerful that NASA recreated it with satellites in 2002 when the originals began to show their age.

NASA's 'Pale Blue Dot' photograph — taken by Voyager 1 on February 14, 1990, from a distance of 6.06 billion kilometers — shows Earth as a fraction of a pixel in a beam of scattered sunlight; Carl Sagan's meditation on the image became one of the most celebrated passages in science writing: 'That's here. That's home. That's us.'

The 'Hubble Deep Field' (1995) — a 10-day exposure of a seemingly blank patch of sky by the Hubble Space Telescope — revealed approximately 3,000 galaxies in an area 1/13,000,000th of the sky's total area; it and its successors (Ultra Deep Field, 2004; Extreme Deep Field, 2012) remain the deepest photographic images ever made, each containing billions of years of cosmic history.

The first photograph of a black hole — the supermassive black hole at the center of galaxy M87, 6.5 billion solar masses at a distance of 55 million light-years — was published on April 10, 2019, by the Event Horizon Telescope collaboration; the image was assembled from data collected by eight radio observatories worldwide, effectively creating an Earth-sized virtual telescope.

The concept of 'photographic truth' has been complicated throughout the medium's history by manipulation — combination printing (1850s), retouching (1860s), Stalin-era removal of political enemies from official photographs, and Photoshop (1990s); the current AI image generation crisis is therefore the latest chapter in a 180-year history of photography's problematic relationship with authenticity.

The first major photographic forgery scandal was the 'Cottingley Fairies' case (1917–1920) — photographs of fairies taken by Frances Griffiths and Elsie Wright that deceived Arthur Conan Doyle and numerous photographic experts; the girls used paper cutout fairies from a children's book, yet leading experts' belief in their authenticity demonstrated how photography's presumed objectivity could override critical thinking.

The 1994 Time magazine cover showing O.J. Simpson's mug shot with darkened skin was one of the most discussed examples of racial manipulation in photojournalism; the magazine's photo editor digitally darkened Simpson's face to make him appear more menacing, demonstrating how apparently objective documentary photographs can be manipulated to reinforce racial prejudice.

The 'World Press Photo of the Year' has been stripped from winners three times for digital manipulation (2013, 2015, 2017), reflecting both the ease of digital manipulation and the organization's ongoing effort to maintain documentary standards; the contests' evolving technical verification procedures — including RAW file checks and metadata analysis — illustrate photojournalism's technical response to the manipulation crisis.

Adobe Photoshop, first released for Macintosh in 1990 (version 1.0), was developed by Thomas and John Knoll; 'photoshopping' has become a generic verb meaning any digital image manipulation, joining 'xerox' and 'google' as brand names absorbed into common language; Adobe's 2021 'Content Authenticity Initiative' aims to attach verifiable metadata to authentic photographs to counter AI-generated images.

AI image generation models including DALL-E (2021), Midjourney (2022), and Stable Diffusion (2022) can produce photorealistic images from text descriptions; their training on billions of copyrighted photographs without permission has led to class-action lawsuits by photographers and triggered the ongoing debate about whether AI-generated images should be eligible for photojournalism prizes.

The first AI-generated image to win a photography competition — Boris Eldagsen's 'Pseudoamnesia: The Electrician' at the 2023 Sony World Photography Awards — was withdrawn by the artist himself when he revealed the image was AI-generated; he stated his submission was a 'cheeky provocation' to start a conversation about whether AI images should compete with photographs.

The concept of 'surveillance photography' — photographs taken without subjects' knowledge or consent — has existed since street photography began in the 1880s, but the combination of ubiquitous CCTV, smartphone cameras, facial recognition AI, and social media has created an environment in which virtually every public movement is photographically recorded; privacy scholars describe this as a fundamental shift in human social existence.

The 'camera phone revolution' is typically dated to the introduction of the Sharp J-SH04 in Japan (November 2000), the first commercially available camera phone; within 15 years, camera phones had made photographers out of every mobile phone owner, increasing the number of photographs taken annually from approximately 85 billion (2000) to over 1.4 trillion (2020).

The motion picture standardization of 24 frames per second was established in the late 1920s when sound synchronization required a fixed frame rate; James Cameron shot 'The Hobbit' (2012) and 'Gemini Man' (2019) at 48fps and 120fps respectively, to mixed critical reception — most viewers described the higher frame rate as 'soap opera effect,' preferring 24fps's familiar aesthetic of slight motion blur.

The aspect ratio of 2.35:1 (now often 2.39:1), called CinemaScope or Scope, was introduced by 20th Century Fox in 1953 as a competitive response to television; 'The Robe' (1953) was the first CinemaScope film and its wide canvas encouraged directors to compose differently — long horizontal staging rather than the theatrical blocking suited to the old 1.37:1 Academy ratio.

Dolby Atmos, introduced in 2012 with the animated film 'Brave,' is an object-based audio format that places individual sounds in three-dimensional space — including overhead speakers — rather than fixed channels; its use of up to 64 speakers in theaters creates immersive soundscapes impossible with traditional 5.1 or 7.1 surround; Christopher Nolan's films are considered benchmark demonstrations of Atmos capabilities.

The invention of the optical soundtrack — a photographic recording of sound waves printed on the edge of film — by Lee De Forest in 1923 preceded The Jazz Singer (1927) by four years; De Forest's 'Phonofilm' system was rejected by studios, and it was Western Electric's Vitaphone (disc-based sound) that the studios adopted, delaying optical sound's commercial success.

The THX sound certification program, developed by Tomlinson Holman at Lucasfilm in 1983 for the theatrical release of 'Return of the Jedi,' established minimum technical standards for cinema sound reproduction — room acoustics, screen, and playback equipment — creating consistent audio experiences across different theaters that had previously varied enormously in sound quality.

Bernard Herrmann's score for 'Psycho' (1960) — composed entirely for strings — creates its psychological horror through dissonant harmonics, sharp rhythmic punctuation, and the iconic shrieking strings of the shower scene; Hitchcock initially wanted no music for the shower scene, and Herrmann's music was so transformative that Hitchcock doubled his fee and acknowledged the score's indispensable contribution.

John Williams has composed scores for six of the ten highest-grossing films of all time and has received more Oscar nominations than any other living person (54 nominations as of 2023, winning five); his leitmotif-based compositional style, derived from Richard Wagner via Erich Wolfgang Korngold, created a template for epic film scoring still widely imitated.

source.name: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

text: Ennio Morricone composed over 400 scores across a 60-year career, creating sonic identities for spaghetti Westerns ('The Good, the Bad and the Ugly,' 1966), giallo horror ('The Bird with the Crystal Plumage,' 1970), and prestige drama ('The Mission,' 1986); he was awarded an honorary Oscar in 2007 and a competitive Oscar at age 87 for Tarantino's 'The Hateful Eight' (2015).

source.name: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

text: Nino Rota composed scores for all of Fellini's films and the Godfather trilogy; his iconic Godfather waltz theme was initially rejected by Paramount executives as too simple and was kept only because Coppola insisted; the melody has since become the most recognized film theme in history after John Williams's 'Star Wars.''

Foley art — the reproduction of everyday sound effects added to film in post-production — was invented by Jack Foley at Universal Pictures in the late 1920s; Foley artists create sounds including footsteps, clothing rustle, and fight effects in real-time while watching the film, using creative objects (celery for bone-breaking sounds, raw chicken for punching) to create convincing audio.

Walter Murch, film editor and sound designer for 'Apocalypse Now' (1979) and 'The English Patient' (1996), articulated the 'rule of six' for editing decisions — prioritizing emotion, story, rhythm, eye trace, two-dimensional plane, and three-dimensional space in that order of importance; his book 'In the Blink of an Eye' (1995) is the most influential guide to film editing theory.
tags: in the blink of an eye

text: Thelma Schoonmaker, Martin Scorsese's editor since 'Raging Bull' (1980), has won three Academy Awards for Editing — for 'Raging Bull' (1980), 'The Aviator' (2004), and 'The Departed' (2006); her collaboration with Scorsese, spanning over 40 years, is cinema's longest director-editor partnership and is credited with shaping the kinetic, rhythmically complex editing style of his major films.

source.name: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

text: The Avid Media Composer, introduced in 1989, was the first digital non-linear editing system widely adopted by Hollywood; it replaced the physically demanding Moviola flatbed editing where film was literally cut and spliced with tape; the transition to digital editing changed not just the process but the aesthetics of editing — making complex multi-track sequences and real-time previewing possible for the first time.

The first completely CGI character in a major Hollywood film was the 'Stained Glass Knight' in 'Young Sherlock Holmes' (1985), created by Lucasfilm's graphics division (which became Pixar); the breakthrough 'morphing' effect in 'Willow' (1988) and 'The Abyss' (1989), and the liquid-metal T-1000 in 'Terminator 2: Judgment Day' (1991), each marked progressive milestones in photorealistic CGI.

Motion capture technology — recording actors' physical performances digitally to animate CGI characters — was used to create Gollum in 'The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers' (2002); Andy Serkis's performance-capture work as Gollum, Caesar in 'Rise of the Planet of the Apes,' and Kong in 'King Kong' established 'performance capture' as a recognized acting discipline, though one still ineligible for Academy Award consideration.

The 'uncanny valley' — the unease humans feel when CGI human faces approach but do not perfectly replicate reality — was first observed in robotics by Masahiro Mori (1970) and became a major problem in digital human rendering in films including 'The Polar Express' (2004) and 'Beowulf' (2007); ILM's breakthrough in rendering Paul Walker's digital face for 'Furious 7' (2015) significantly advanced solutions to the problem.

The 'deepfake' technology — using AI to swap faces in video footage convincingly — was first widely demonstrated in 2017 when Reddit user 'deepfakes' posted AI-generated celebrity face swaps; it immediately raised concerns about both political disinformation (fabricated statements by world leaders) and non-consensual intimate images; it also has legitimate applications in film de-aging and dubbing.

The de-aging of actors using digital visual effects — used extensively in 'The Irishman' (2019, Scorsese), 'Captain Marvel' (2019), and 'Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny' (2023) — creates ethical questions about whether audiences are watching genuine performances or constructed simulations; critics argue that a 30-year-old digital Robert De Niro is a different performance than a 75-year-old Robert De Niro would have given.

The virtual production technique of using large LED screen walls ('volumes') to display moving backgrounds while actors perform in real-time — pioneered by Industrial Light & Magic for 'The Mandalorian' (2019) using a system called StageCraft — has transformed film and television production by replacing location shoots and green screen with photorealistic in-camera environments.

The 'Star Wars Holiday Special' (1978) is widely considered the worst major studio television production ever made — a two-hour CBS special featuring the extended Wookiee family of Chewbacca that George Lucas has tried to suppress; it has never been officially released on home video, making bootleg VHS copies and YouTube clips the only means of viewing what critics call 'a legend of cinematic catastrophe.'

The 'Final Cut' controversy involves directors' right to their preferred version of a film against studios' right to re-edit for commercial release; Francis Ford Coppola restored 49 minutes cut from 'The Godfather Part III' (re-released as 'Mario Puzo's The Godfather, Coda' in 2020), and Ridley Scott has released at least 4 distinct versions of 'Blade Runner' (1982), raising questions about which version represents the 'authentic' film.

The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences' museum — the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures in Los Angeles — opened in September 2021 after 17 years of planning and $388 million in construction costs; it is the largest museum in the world dedicated to the history and science of film, housing the Barbra Streisand Campus and the Shirley Temple Archive.

Shirley Temple, the biggest box-office star in the world from 1935 to 1938, received a special juvenile Academy Award in 1935 at age six — one of the few honorary Oscars given to a child performer; her transition to adult roles was largely unsuccessful, demonstrating the industry's difficulty imagining child stars as adult actors.

source.name: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

text: The Hollywood Walk of Fame on Hollywood Boulevard and Vine Street, established in 1958, has over 2,700 stars honoring entertainment industry figures; the first star was dedicated to Joanne Woodward on February 8, 1960; honorees must be invited by the Chamber of Commerce and typically pay a $50,000 maintenance fee.

The Screen Actors Guild (SAG), founded in 1933 during a Hollywood actors' wage dispute, merged with the American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (AFTRA) in 2012 to form SAG-AFTRA; the combined union represents approximately 160,000 media professionals and its annual Screen Actors Guild Awards are considered an important predictor of Oscar results.

The Writers Guild of America (WGA) strike of 2023, combined with the SAG-AFTRA strike (the first combined writers-actors strike since 1960), halted Hollywood production for five months — the longest work stoppage in the industry since the 1988 writers' strike; the 2023 strikes were largely about residuals from streaming and protections against AI replacing human writers.

The Motion Picture Association (MPA), founded in 1922 as the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America by Will Hays, created the first content rating system (initially the Hays Code, then the current letter rating system from 1968) and lobbies for film industry interests including copyright protection internationally; the MPA represents major studios including Disney, Universal, Sony, Paramount, and Warner Bros.

The National Film Registry, maintained by the Library of Congress under the National Film Preservation Act (1988), selects 25 films annually deemed 'culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant' for preservation; as of 2024 it contains 900 films ranging from Hollywood classics to underground experimental works and amateur home movies.

The European Film Awards, founded in 1988 by Ingmar Bergman and presented annually by the European Film Academy, are the continent's equivalent of the Oscars; winners have included films from all major European cinema traditions, and the 'European Film of the Year' has been won by films from Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, and Hungary among others.

The film 'Cleopatra' (1963), starring Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton, cost $44 million — the equivalent of over $400 million in 2024 dollars — nearly bankrupting 20th Century Fox and remaining the most expensive film ever made in inflation-adjusted terms at the time; it became financially successful only after decades of television licensing.

The Coen Brothers — Joel and Ethan Coen — have both jointly and separately directed some of cinema's most distinctive genre films, collecting Academy Awards including Best Picture, Director, Adapted Screenplay, and Original Screenplay; their creative partnership, in which they share all directorial and writing credits, is unique in Hollywood history for its longevity and consistent critical recognition.

source.name: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

text: Agnès Varda, co-founder of the French New Wave's Left Bank branch, was the first woman director to receive an honorary Palme d'Or at Cannes (2015) and an honorary Academy Award (2017); her late-career documentary 'Faces Places' (2017, co-directed with photographer JR), made when she was 88, received an Oscar nomination and demonstrated that significant filmmaking is possible at any age.

The Bechdel Test, named after cartoonist Alison Bechdel who described it in a 1985 comic strip, asks three questions of a film: does it have two named female characters who talk to each other about something other than a man? A majority of Hollywood films fail this minimal standard; the test's viral adoption as a metric has influenced studios to track and improve female representation.

The first woman to direct a feature film was Alice Guy-Blaché, a French director who began making films for Gaumont in 1896 — one year after cinema's invention — and founded her own American studio, Solax Company, in 1910; her prolific output of over 1,000 films was largely forgotten until feminist film historians recovered her work in the 1980s.

Kathryn Bigelow became the first woman to win the Academy Award for Best Director for 'The Hurt Locker' (2010), defeating her ex-husband James Cameron's 'Avatar' — the film she beat had been the highest-grossing film of all time; only seven women have been nominated for Best Director in Oscar history as of 2024.

source.name: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

text: The Bechdel-Wallace Test has spawned related metrics: the DuVernay Test (whether African-American characters are depicted as fully realized humans rather than stereotypes), the Riz Test (for Muslim representation), and the Villareal Test (for Latino representation); collectively these tools have made representation in film empirically measurable and have influenced studio diversity initiatives.

The 'Hattie McDaniel Problem' — named for the first Black Oscar winner (Best Supporting Actress for 'Gone with the Wind,' 1940) who was segregated to a side table at the ceremony and could not sit with the film's white cast — has been used by scholars to discuss how Hollywood simultaneously exploited and excluded Black talent; McDaniel was barred from attending the Atlanta premiere of her own film.

source.name: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

text: Sidney Poitier won the Academy Award for Best Actor for 'Lilies of the Field' (1963) — the first Black person to receive a competitive acting Oscar — and along with Harry Belafonte single-handedly carried the financial risk of several civil-rights-era films; Poitier's insistence on playing dignified, non-stereotyped characters permanently changed how Hollywood depicted Black men.

source.name: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

text: Spike Lee's 'Do the Right Thing' (1989) — which depicted a race riot in Brooklyn ending in the death of a Black man at the hands of police — was widely criticized at its release for its supposed incitement; its failure to receive Best Picture or Director nominations at the 1990 Oscars (which went to 'Driving Miss Daisy') is now considered one of the greatest oversights in Oscar history.

Ryan Coogler's 'Black Panther' (2018) was the first superhero film nominated for Best Picture at the Academy Awards and grossed $1.35 billion worldwide; its unprecedented box-office success with a predominantly Black cast definitively disproved the 'Black films don't travel internationally' assumption that had constrained Hollywood casting decisions for decades.

The Blaxploitation film cycle (1971–1979) — which began with Gordon Parks Sr.'s 'Shaft' (1971) and Melvin Van Peebles' 'Sweet Sweetback's Baadasssss Song' (1971) — was controversial both for providing Black audiences with Black heroes and for relying on stereotyped villains and sexual imagery; it provided the first sustained employment for Black directors, actors, and composers in Hollywood.

The Western genre — the dominant American film genre from the silent era through the 1960s — went through multiple stylistic periods: the classic Western (John Ford, 1930s–1950s), the revisionist psychological Western (Anthony Mann, 1950s), the Italian Spaghetti Western (Leone, 1960s), and the 'twilight Western' (Peckinpah, 1970s) that acknowledged the mythology's exhaustion while continuing to use it.

Sam Peckinpah's 'The Wild Bunch' (1969), containing 3,643 cuts in 144 minutes (more than any previous Hollywood film), used slow motion — up to 120 frames per second — to choreograph violence with balletic aesthetic appreciation; its simultaneous condemnation and aestheticization of violence established the modern action film's grammar and remains profoundly controversial.

John Woo's Hong Kong action films — 'A Better Tomorrow' (1986), 'The Killer' (1989), 'Hard Boiled' (1992) — created the 'heroic bloodshed' genre using slow motion, dual-pistol aesthetics, and operatic sentimentality that influenced action cinema worldwide; his Hollywood films ('Face/Off' 1997, 'Mission: Impossible 2' 2000) brought these techniques to global audiences while losing some of their original emotional intensity.

Park Chan-wook's 'Oldboy' (2003), winner of the Cannes Grand Prix, is the centerpiece of his 'Vengeance Trilogy' and uses an extreme long-take corridor fight sequence shot in a single take from the side to dramatize exhausted, desperate violence without cinematic glamorization; it became the most influential Asian film on Western action cinema in the 2000s.

Quentin Tarantino's chronologically scrambled narrative in 'Pulp Fiction' (1994) — using non-linear storytelling to create ironic juxtapositions between violence and domesticity — revitalized American independent cinema and demonstrated that sophisticated narrative structure could succeed commercially; the film cost $8 million and grossed $214 million, becoming one of the most profitable independent films ever made.

The 'mockumentary of real events' technique — using fictional documentary framing to present invented events as real — was pushed to its extreme in 'The Blair Witch Project' (1999), which was marketed as footage of genuinely missing students before its theatrical release; its $60,000 production cost and $248 million global gross make it the most profitable film in box-office-to-budget terms in cinema history.

Christopher Nolan's 'Memento' (2000) — narrated backwards in its main timeline so viewers experience events in the same confusing sequence as the amnesiac protagonist — was his breakthrough film made for $9 million; it demonstrated that formally complex narrative structure could attract mainstream audiences and established Nolan's career trajectory toward increasingly ambitious conceptual cinema.

David Lynch's 'Eraserhead' (1977) — his debut feature, shot over five years on weekends using American Film Institute grants — created a nightmare industrial landscape through in-camera practical effects, sound design, and a dreamlike narrative logic that established 'Lynchian' as a recognized aesthetic category meaning dreamlike, unsettling, or surreally disturbing.

Werner Herzog has made over 60 documentary and fiction films and is known for his willingness to place himself and his cast in genuine physical danger — sailing real boats up the Amazon, burying himself in a sand storm, almost drowning cast and crew in 'Fitzcarraldo' (1982) — in pursuit of what he calls 'ecstatic truth' rather than observational documentary realism.

Jean-Luc Godard's 'Breathless' ('À bout de souffle,' 1960) — using a wheelchair as a dolly for tracking shots, natural light, post-synchronized sound, and jump cuts editing — broke so many established filmmaking conventions that each technical 'limitation' became an aesthetic choice; its influence on subsequent cinema is so pervasive that film critics use 'Godardian' as shorthand for self-conscious formal innovation.

The 'long take' or 'sequence shot' — a single uncut shot lasting several minutes — challenges the Kuleshov editing principle by placing all compositional meaning within the frame rather than between cuts; Orson Welles's opening shot of 'Touch of Evil' (1958), a 3.3-minute crane shot across a border crossing, is cinema's most celebrated long take demonstration.

Sam Mendes's '1917' (2019) — designed to appear as a single continuous shot following two WWI soldiers in real-time — required nine months of rehearsal, innovative camera rigging allowing continuous handheld movement with actors across 1.6-kilometer outdoor sets, and hidden cuts disguised by passing through dark tunnels or momentary blackouts; it won three Academy Awards including Cinematography and Visual Effects.

source.name: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

text: Alexander Sokurov's 'Russian Ark' (2002) is the only commercially released feature film shot in a single, genuinely uninterrupted take — 96 minutes through 33 rooms of the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg; it required 867 actors and three orchestras, with the director of photography Tilman Büttner walking backwards through the museum for the entire runtime carrying a digital cinema camera.

Mike Figgis's 'Timecode' (2000) was filmed in a single 93-minute take using four simultaneously recording digital cameras, with the screen split into four quadrants showing the action from each camera simultaneously; actors improvised within a loose framework while Figgis controlled the audio mix live during filming to direct audience attention to whichever quadrant contained the most important action.

The Dogme 95 manifesto, signed by Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg in 1995, required films to be shot on location with no props or sets not found naturally, use only natural light, prohibit non-diegetic music, and be shot handheld — the first 'certified' Dogme film was Vinterberg's 'Festen' (The Celebration, 1998), which won the Jury Prize at Cannes.

The Iranian New Wave, emerging in the late 1960s and revitalized after the 1979 Islamic Revolution, produced internationally celebrated directors including Abbas Kiarostami, Jafar Panahi, and Asghar Farhadi; Farhadi's 'A Separation' (2011) won both the Golden Bear at Berlin and the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, establishing Iranian cinema as among the world's most admired.

Jafar Panahi has directed six internationally acclaimed films while under a 20-year filmmaking ban imposed by the Iranian government following his arrest in 2010; he continued making films secretly, including 'This Is Not a Film' (2011, shot on an iPhone inside his apartment and smuggled out of Iran on a USB drive hidden in a cake), demonstrating cinema's power to resist political suppression.

The Romanian New Wave, emerging in the early 2000s with films by Cristi Puiu, Cristian Mungiu, and Corneliu Porumboiu, uses extremely long takes, naturalistic acting, and minimal camera movement to examine post-communist Romanian society; Mungiu's '4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days' (2007) won the Palme d'Or at Cannes and is widely considered one of the greatest films of the 21st century.

Thailand's 'Apichatpong Weerasethakul' (known as Joe) makes films that blend dreams, ghosts, memory, and waking life without clearly demarcating where one ends and another begins; his 'Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives' (2010) won the Palme d'Or, introducing global audiences to a cinematic vocabulary rooted in Buddhist cosmology and Thai folk tradition.

Hong Sangsoo, the South Korean director, makes films about writers, artists, and directors encountering women in cafes and bars, using repeating structures, mirror scenes, and temporal ambiguity to explore how memory shapes reality; his ultra-low budget approach — typically shooting his own scripts with a tiny crew in real locations — has produced over 30 features recognized at Cannes, Berlin, and Locarno.

Ritwik Ghatak, the Bengali filmmaker whose 'Meghe Dhaka Tara' (1960) and 'Komal Gandhar' (1961) depicted the trauma of India's Partition through expressionist sound design and visceral cinematography, was largely unknown outside India during his lifetime but is now ranked alongside Satyajit Ray as the most important figure in Bengali cinema's golden age.

Luis Buñuel's 'The Exterminating Angel' (1962) — in which upper-class dinner guests find themselves mysteriously unable to leave a drawing room, though no physical barrier prevents them — is the perfect Surrealist allegory of bourgeois social imprisonment; Buñuel made surrealist films over a 50-year career from 'Un Chien Andalou' (1929) through 'That Obscure Object of Desire' (1977).

Pier Paolo Pasolini's final film 'Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom' (1975) — transposing de Sade's novel to fascist Italy and depicting systematic dehumanization through extreme sexual violence — was banned in several countries and remains one of cinema's most disturbing and intellectually serious meditations on power, fascism, and consumerism; Pasolini was murdered the night before its Italian premiere.

Michelangelo Antonioni's 'L'Avventura' (1960) — in which a woman disappears on a volcanic island and is never found, while her friends and lover continue to seek her with diminishing urgency — was booed at its Cannes premiere but won the Jury Prize and is now considered one of cinema's masterpieces for its unprecedented use of narrative absence and empty landscape as psychological states.

Federico Fellini's 'La Dolce Vita' (1960) — set in the decadent celebrity culture of Rome and depicting a journalist's moral drift through a series of spectacular episodes — gave the Italian language the word 'paparazzo' (from a character's name), which subsequently entered global languages to describe aggressive celebrity photographers.

Roberto Rossellini's 'Rome, Open City' (1945), shot in the streets of Rome weeks after the Nazi withdrawal using scavenged film stock, invented Italian Neorealism — a style using non-actors, real locations, natural lighting, and social content — that influenced global art cinema more than any subsequent movement including the French New Wave and Iranian cinema.

Vittorio De Sica's 'Bicycle Thieves' (1948) — in which a father and son search Rome for a stolen bicycle needed for work — used an entirely non-professional cast, actual locations in working-class Rome, and a story of economic desperation to create what many critics consider the perfect Neorealist film; Orson Welles called it the most important film ever made.

Luchino Visconti's 'La Terra Trema' (1948), entirely shot and acted by the fishing community of Aci Trezza, Sicily, in their Sicilian dialect, was so linguistically inaccessible that it required Italian subtitles for mainland Italian audiences; it represents the extreme of Neorealist commitment to authentic social documentation rather than dramatic accessibility.

The 'Cinema Novo' movement in Brazil (1960s–1970s), whose motto was 'a camera in the hand and an idea in the head,' produced politically engaged films by Glauber Rocha ('Black God, White Devil,' 1964; 'Antonio das Mortes,' 1969) and Nelson Pereira dos Santos that combined Neorealist social content with avant-garde formal experimentation influenced by Brecht and Eisenstein.

African cinema was largely colonially controlled until the Senegalese filmmaker Ousmane Sembène — trained in Moscow — made 'Borom Sarret' (1963), Africa's first Sub-Saharan feature film by an African director; his subsequent films in Wolof and French addressed colonialism, patriarchy, and tradition, establishing him as the 'Father of African Cinema.'

The Australian New Wave of the 1970s, funded by the Australian Film Commission established in 1975, produced internationally successful films including 'Picnic at Hanging Rock' (1975), 'Gallipoli' (1981), and 'Mad Max' (1979) that established a distinctive Australian national cinema and launched the international careers of directors Peter Weir, Bruce Beresford, and George Miller.

The 'Bollywood formula' of song-and-dance sequences interspersed through melodramatic narratives derives from Indian theatrical traditions (nautanki, jatra) and the Parsi theater rather than from Hollywood; the 'item number' — a song performed by a special guest actor not in the main cast — has been a feature of Hindi commercial cinema since the 1950s and continues to be an expected element of mainstream Indian films.

The Kannada film industry (Sandalwood), based in Bengaluru, produced 'K.G.F: Chapter 1' (2018), which was dubbed into four languages and broke several box-office records in South India; its sequel 'K.G.F: Chapter 2' (2022), with a worldwide gross of over $270 million, demonstrated that South Indian regional cinema had become globally competitive with Hindi-language Bollywood films.

Telugu cinema's 'RRR' (2022), directed by S.S. Rajamouli, grossed over $170 million worldwide and won the Academy Award for Best Original Song ('Naatu Naatu') — the first Indian film to win a competitive Oscar; its success in Japan, North America, and Europe demonstrated that non-English language commercial blockbusters could achieve global theatrical success without dubbing.

source.name: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

text: The Chinese 'Fifth Generation' of filmmakers — Zhang Yimou, Chen Kaige, and others who graduated from the Beijing Film Academy's first class after the Cultural Revolution (1978) — used allegory, landscape, and color symbolism to address China's historical traumas; Zhang Yimou's 'Red Sorghum' (1988) and 'Raise the Red Lantern' (1991) introduced Chinese art cinema to international audiences.

Edward Yang's 'Yi Yi' (2000) — a three-hour portrait of a Taipei family over a year — is widely considered the greatest Taiwanese film ever made; Yang died of cancer in 2007 at 59 without making another film after 'Yi Yi,' and his restricted filmography (7 features over 20 years) represents one of cinema's great losses; Criterion's restoration introduced his work to new audiences.

Hou Hsiao-hsien's slow cinema — extremely long takes, distant framings, elliptical narratives — in films like 'A City of Sadness' (1989, about Taiwan's 2-28 Massacre) and 'The Assassin' (2015) created a visual approach so distinctive that 'Hou-style' has become a recognized term in film scholarship for quiet observation of daily life with no explanatory narration.

Japan's Toho Studios created Godzilla ('Gojira') in 1954 as a direct allegory of nuclear anxiety following the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings and the Lucky Dragon 5 incident (a Japanese fishing vessel irradiated by a US hydrogen bomb test); the original Godzilla is explicitly a creation of atomic testing, and the metaphor was diluted in subsequent sequels.

Yasujiro Ozu's films — made with a low camera position (called 'tatami shot' for the eye level of a seated person on a tatami mat), minimal cutting, 'pillow shots' of empty spaces between scenes, and stories of family disruption — use formal restrictions to create extraordinary emotional depth; 'Tokyo Story' (1953) is regularly voted among the top three greatest films in Sight & Sound polls.

The Sight & Sound magazine poll of the greatest films of all time, conducted every decade since 1952 by the British Film Institute, is considered the most authoritative critical consensus in cinema; 'Vertigo' displaced 'Citizen Kane' from the top position in 2012 after 50 years, and Chantal Akerman's 'Jeanne Dielman, 23, quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles' (1975) topped the 2022 poll for the first time.

Chantal Akerman's 'Jeanne Dielman, 23, quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles' (1975) — a 3.5-hour real-time observation of a Belgian housewife's three-day domestic routine, ending in sudden violence — uses feminist durational filmmaking to make visible the invisible labor of housework; its 2022 selection as the greatest film of all time by Sight & Sound critics was hailed as a landmark acknowledgment of women's cinema.

The Criterion Collection, founded in 1984, pioneered laserdisc and DVD releases with restored transfers, director commentaries, and supplementary essays that elevated home video from a movie-delivery mechanism to a film culture platform; its distinctive black-and-white spine design and rigorous curation have made it the most influential independent distributor of art and world cinema in America.

Home video — the VHS cassette format introduced by JVC in 1976 — transformed cinema's economics by creating a secondary revenue stream that eventually exceeded theatrical box office for studios; the Betamax-vs-VHS format war (1975–1988) was won by VHS despite Betamax's superior technical quality, demonstrating that marketing, duration capacity, and distribution matter more than performance in consumer technology wars.

Blockbuster Video, founded in 1985 and at its peak operating 9,000 stores worldwide, became the dominant home video rental chain before being bankrupted by Netflix's DVD-by-mail model (2007) and streaming (2013); the last remaining Blockbuster store (in Bend, Oregon) has become a cultural landmark and the subject of documentary 'The Last Blockbuster' (2020).

Netflix, founded as a DVD-by-mail service in 1997 and transitioning to streaming in 2007, became the world's largest subscription streaming platform with over 270 million subscribers by 2024; its algorithmic personalization and investment in original content ('House of Cards,' 2013, its first original series) transformed both television and film production, distribution, and audience behavior globally.

The digital projection revolution — transitioning cinemas from 35mm film to digital (DCP) projection — was substantially complete in the United States by 2013 and globally by 2015, ending over a century of projecting physical film; 35mm projection is now used exclusively in a small number of revival houses and by directors including Quentin Tarantino who insist on photochemical cinema.

Christopher Nolan shot 'Oppenheimer' (2023) partly on IMAX film cameras — the first time that large-format film cameras were used for dramatized narrative sequences in IMAX — achieving a resolution and grain quality impossible with digital sensors; the film grossed $953 million worldwide while being shot primarily on film, demonstrating that photochemical cinema remains commercially viable.

The 'analog photography revival' — Kodak's Ektachrome revival (2018), the growth of film photography among Gen Z, and the record sales of film cameras at auction — reflects a broader cultural reaction against digital perfectibility; Kodak reported film sales growth of over 50% between 2015 and 2022, and camera retailers including B&H Photo noted that film camera sales exceeded forecasts every year from 2017.

Lomography — the international movement promoting casual, imprecise, lo-fi photography using cheap plastic cameras like the Holga and Lomo LC-A — emerged from Vienna in 1992 when students discovered the Soviet Lomo LC-A camera; its Ten Golden Rules ('Don't think, just shoot'; 'Always shoot from the hip'; 'Don't worry about the rules') created a photographic philosophy antithetical to precision and control.

The International Photography Hall of Fame and Museum (IPHF), established in 1965 in St. Louis and later relocated to Oklahoma City, inducts photographers who have made outstanding contributions; it recognized Ansel Adams, Henri Cartier-Bresson, Alfred Stieglitz, and Dorothea Lange among its inaugural honorees, establishing a photography canon that universities and museums have built upon.

The daguerreotype's inability to be reproduced — each daguerreotype is a unique object, not a print from a negative — made it closer to a mirror than a photograph in the philosophical sense; this uniqueness has made daguerreotypes highly collectible, with early examples by prominent photographers including Samuel Morse (who photographed his daughters) selling for over $100,000.

Imogen Cunningham, a founding member of Group f/64, began photographing in 1901 and continued until her death in 1976 at age 93 — a photographic career spanning 75 years that traversed pictorialism, modernism, street photography, and portraiture; she photographed everyone from her naked husband to Cary Grant to Martha Graham, leaving over 30,000 negatives.

Paul Strand, whose 1916–1917 photographs in Alfred Stieglitz's 'Camera Work' magazine — showing abstract designs of shadows, fences, and street people shot with a fake lens to prevent subjects knowing they were being photographed — are considered the first modern photographs, breaking definitively with pictorialism through their formal abstraction and social engagement.

Man Ray's rayographs — objects placed directly on photosensitive paper and exposed to light — and his solarized photographs (partially exposed to light during development, creating a partial tone reversal) were created in the darkroom as experiments in visual abstraction; his use of photographic technique purely for aesthetic effect without a camera established darkroom experimentation as a legitimate photographic practice.

August Sander's 'People of the Twentieth Century' — a planned encyclopedic portrait of German society organized by occupation and social class, begun in 1910 — was interrupted when Nazis burned copies of his 1929 book 'Face of Our Time'; his systematic, frontal, neutral portrait style directly influenced the Becher school's typological photography and Andy Warhol's 'Screen Tests.'

László Moholy-Nagy's photograms, photo montages, and time-exposure light paintings at the Bauhaus (1923–1928) articulated 'the new vision' — using photography's mechanical, process-based nature to reveal optical phenomena impossible to human perception; his influence on graphic design, typography, and photography education through the Chicago Institute of Design extended American modernism.

The 'New Vision' photography of the 1920s–1930s — including Alexander Rodchenko's extreme oblique angles, bird's-eye views, and worm's-eye perspectives — was driven by a constructivist belief that the camera should show the world in ways the eye could not; Rodchenko's 1928 photograph of a Pioneer Girl looking up from a steep diagonal angle is one of the most reproduced images in the history of photography.

The 'straight photography' aesthetic championed by Group f/64 was challenged from the 1970s by 'staged photography' — images set up rather than found — practiced by Cindy Sherman, Jeff Wall, and Gregory Crewdson; Jeff Wall's large lightbox photographs, meticulously staged to resemble news photographs, raised fundamental questions about documentary photography's special claim to truth.

Gregory Crewdson's large-scale photographs of American suburban uncanny — elaborate productions involving Hollywood-scale lighting crews, constructed sets, and actors in strange, ambiguous tableaux — have been compared to Hopper paintings and Spielberg films; each image can take weeks to produce and costs over $100,000 to execute, challenging the assumed economy of photography versus painting.

The carte-de-visite portrait photograph created the first photographic celebrity culture in the 1860s; photographs of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert sold millions of copies throughout the British Empire, and carte-de-visite albums including images of President Lincoln were produced as commercial products across the United States, establishing the connection between photography and celebrity worship that culminates in today's influencer economy.

Yoko Ono's 'Instruction Paintings' (1960s) included photographic instructions for conceptual art actions that may or may not be executed; her 'Grapefruit' (1964) book of instructions anticipated participatory and conceptual art photography; she is rarely credited as an influence on contemporary participatory and social practice photography despite her foundational role.

The 'landscape photography' tradition — from Carleton Watkins's mammoth-plate photographs of Yosemite (1861) that helped convince Congress to protect the valley, through Ansel Adams's 'Sierra Nevada' series — has been explicitly political, using beauty as an argument for environmental protection; contemporary photographers including Sebastião Salgado and Edward Burtynsky continue this tradition in both its preservationist and critical modes.

Aerial photography was first performed by French photographer and balloonist Gaspard-Félix Tournachon ('Nadar') in 1858 from a tethered balloon over Bièvre, France; his photographs do not survive, but the technique he pioneered was immediately adopted for military reconnaissance and mapmaking, establishing the vertical perspective that would later define satellite photography and Google Earth.

text: Google Street View, launched in 2007 with coverage of five US cities, has photographed over 10 million miles of roads in 93 countries — creating the largest continuous photographic record of the world's surface ever assembled; its combination of machine-made documentary imagery, privacy controversies (capturing inadvertent nude images, crime in progress, and private medical facilities), and cultural fascination has made it a unique form of photography.

The 'decisive moment' concept applied to cinema is the cut — the specific frame at which an edit occurs; Walter Murch observed that the perfect cut point is often one frame before the obvious choice, creating a 'subliminal advance' that the brain processes as smooth continuity; professional editors work frame-by-frame (at 1/24 second resolution) to find these optimal moments within a range typically spanning 3–5 frames.

The 'match cut' — cutting between two shots with similar shapes, colors, or movements to create visual continuity and symbolic connection — is exemplified by Stanley Kubrick's cut in '2001: A Space Odyssey' (1968) from a bone thrown into the air to a spinning space station: the most celebrated match cut in cinema history, spanning 4 million years of human technological evolution in a single edit.

The 'jump cut' — removing a portion of a shot and cutting to the same subject from a slightly different angle, creating a visual discontinuity — was used systematically by Jean-Luc Godard in 'Breathless' (1960) as a conscious aesthetic choice rather than a technical error; before Godard, jump cuts were considered mistakes to be hidden by cutting to a different subject between the two versions of the same shot.

The '180-degree rule' of continuity editing — keeping all shots of a scene on the same side of an imaginary line connecting two characters, ensuring consistent screen direction — is one of the first principles taught in film schools; crossing the line creates spatial disorientation; directors including Kubrick, Ozu, and Godard deliberately cross it for psychological and formal effects.

The 'shot-reverse-shot' pattern — alternating between two characters facing each other, each shot from behind the other character's shoulder — is cinema's most fundamental convention for dialogue scenes; it creates psychological intimacy by placing the camera in the physical space of the character being listened to; every conversation scene in mainstream cinema uses this pattern.

The 'establishing shot' — a wide view of a location that orients viewers to space before cutting to closer shots of action within it — derives from theatrical practice of showing the set before actors enter; Sergio Leone subverted the convention in 'Once Upon a Time in the West' (1968) by beginning with extreme close-ups of villains' faces, withholding spatial orientation to create menace.
