The 'film school' as an institution dedicated to educating directors, cinematographers, editors, and other film professionals emerged in the Soviet Union in 1919 (VGIK, the world's oldest film school) and spread to Europe and America in the 1950s–60s; the AFI Conservatory (1969), NYU's Tisch School (1965), USC School of Cinematic Arts (1929, the oldest in the US), and UCLA Film School form the core American film education infrastructure.

The 'spec script' system — in which screenwriters write full scripts without commission, hoping to sell them to studios — emerged in Hollywood in the 1980s when the Studios began reading unsolicited material; spec script sales can reach millions for A-list writers; the spec script auction of 'The Basic Instinct' for $3 million in 1990 transformed the screenwriting market and established the 'spec script boom' of the 1990s.

The 'three-act structure' dominant in Hollywood screenwriting — setup, confrontation, resolution — derives from Aristotle's 'Poetics' through Syd Field's 'Screenplay' (1979), which was the first systematic guide to Hollywood narrative structure; Field's identification of 'plot points' at pages 25 and 75 has been so influential that studio development executives literally count pages to verify structural conformity.

The 'Save the Cat' beat sheet, created by screenwriter Blake Snyder in his 2005 book of the same name, specifies 15 story beats at precise page counts for a 110-page screenplay; it became the dominant Hollywood development template, with critics arguing that its ubiquity has made studio films structurally identical and indistinguishable; filmmakers including Christopher McQuarrie and William Goldman have criticized it for homogenizing storytelling.

The 'test screening' system — showing films to sample audiences before release to gauge reactions and inform edits — was introduced by producer Arthur Loew at MGM in the 1940s; the infamous re-cut of 'Brazil' (1985) by Universal chairman Sid Sheinberg based on negative test screenings, producing a 'Love Conquers All' happy-ending version against director Terry Gilliam's wishes, became cinema's most famous test screening controversy.

The 'trailer' for a film — a short promotional excerpt shown before the main feature — was first used by Paramount in 1913 to advertise a Broadway musical; the term 'trailer' comes from the practice of attaching the promotional reel to the end ('trailing') of the main film print; contemporary film trailers are so precisely engineered for emotional manipulation that 'trailer music' has become its own distinct commercial music genre.

The 'product placement' in cinema — paid insertion of brand products into film narratives — was formalized when Hershey's saw sales increase 65% after Reese's Pieces appeared in 'E.T.' (1982); product placement is now a multi-billion dollar industry in which brands pay $50,000–$500,000 per placement, with the most prominent placements (driving a specific car, drinking a branded beverage) often appearing in multiple shots.

The 'making of' documentary genre — behind-the-scenes footage of film production, now standard as home video bonus content — was pioneered by Les Blank's documentary 'Burden of Dreams' (1982), which recorded the nightmarish production of Werner Herzog's 'Fitzcarraldo' in the Amazon; it established that the story behind the film could be as compelling as the film itself and inspired the entire 'bonus content' DVD industry.

The 'director's commentary' on DVD — allowing filmmakers to explain their creative decisions while the film plays — was invented for the Criterion Collection's LaserDisc release of 'King Kong' (1984) with commentary by Ronald Haver; it transformed home video from passive viewing to film education, and over 40 years has accumulated a vast oral history of filmmaking from directors including Kubrick collaborators who would not otherwise have been interviewed.

The 'Academy Film Archive,' established in 1991, holds over 215,000 titles including motion pictures, sound recordings, and production elements from Hollywood's history; as the repository of films donated by studios and filmmakers and the administrator of the National Film Registry's preservation funding, it is the most important institution for preserving American cinema's legacy.

The 'nitrate film fire' at the Cinémathèque de Toulouse warehouse in 1997 destroyed approximately 4,000 films from the world's third-largest film archive; the Buenos Aires film archive fire (1969) destroyed 40% of Argentina's film heritage; and the MGM fire in Culver City (1967) destroyed thousands of pre-1940 films — collectively these and other fires represent civilization's single greatest cultural loss in the 20th century.

source.name: Fédération Internationale des Archives du Film

text: The 'digital rot' problem in cinema — the obsolescence of file formats, storage media, and playback systems — threatens digital films more severely than well-stored film negatives; a 35mm negative from 1950 properly stored remains playable on equipment built in any decade, while a digital film from 2000 encoded in a now-obsolete format on a now-obsolete storage medium may be effectively unplayable despite being only 25 years old.

The 'Sight & Sound' critics' poll of greatest films, which surveys over 1,600 critics and filmmakers every decade, has become self-fulfilling: films near the top receive more preservation funding, restoration attention, and distribution support, which makes them more accessible and familiar to subsequent voters; the 2022 poll was notable for including more films by women and non-Western directors than any previous edition.

The 'FIAF' (Fédération Internationale des Archives du Film), founded in 1938 in Paris, coordinates film preservation efforts among 180 member archives in 80 countries; its Technical Commission establishes digitization standards, and its journal and conferences have created an international community of practice for film preservation that enables archives to share expertise across political boundaries.

source.name: Fédération Internationale des Archives du Film

text: The 'Sundance Film Festival's' original purpose was to attract Hollywood productions to film in Utah; Robert Redford's involvement transformed it into an independent film showcase; the festival's buyer-seller dynamic — distribution companies acquiring films for millions — was established when 'sex, lies, and videotape' (1989) sold to Miramax for $1 million, the highest price paid for an independent film at that time.

Harvey Weinstein's sexual abuse of actresses, publicized in 2017 through investigations by The New York Times and The New Yorker, triggered the global #MeToo movement; the subsequent Academy Award membership reforms (adding 928 new members in 2016, pledging parity by 2020) and the disqualification of convicted abusers from consideration have structurally changed Hollywood's power dynamics, though critics debate whether changes have been deep enough.

source.name: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

text: The 'LGBTQ+ New Queer Cinema' movement of the early 1990s — triggered by Todd Haynes's 'Poison' (1991), Gus Van Sant's 'My Own Private Idaho' (1991), and Gregg Araki's 'The Living End' (1992) — used low-budget, formally radical aesthetics to represent queer lives during the AIDS crisis; the movement's institutional recognition came from Todd Haynes's later work 'Carol' (2015) receiving six Academy Award nominations.

The 'J-horror' (Japanese horror) genre, established by 'Ringu' (1998) and 'Ju-On: The Grudge' (2002), used still, white-faced female ghosts with long black hair obscuring their faces as a visual trope derived from Japanese theatrical tradition (Noh and Kabuki ghosts); Hollywood's 'The Ring' (2002) and 'The Grudge' (2004) remakes introduced J-horror aesthetics to Western audiences and spawned their own subgenres.

The 'mumblecore' movement — low-budget American independent films of the 2000s characterized by improvised dialogue, non-professional or unknown actors, and minimal plots about young adults navigating relationships — was named by sound editor Eric Masunaga at the 2005 SXSW Festival; directors Joe Swanberg, Andrew Bujalski, and the Duplass brothers pioneered the form before transitioning to mainstream productions.

The 'extreme long shot' — placing subjects so far away they become part of the landscape — has been used by directors including Sergio Leone (the vast desert spaces in 'Once Upon a Time in the West') and Terrence Malick (tiny human figures against enormous natural backdrops in 'Days of Heaven') to express existential diminishment; it is the cinematic equivalent of the Romantic painting tradition of the 'sublime.'

Wes Anderson's visual style — symmetrical compositions with centered subjects, flat graphic staging, pastel color palettes, deadpan performances, and precise musical timing — is so recognizable that his aesthetic has been widely imitated on TikTok's 'Wes Anderson aesthetic' trend, in which users film mundane events in his style; it is one of the few contemporary directorial aesthetics immediately recognizable to non-cinephiles.

The 'pan-and-scan' format used for decades when broadcasting widescreen films on television systematically removed 40–50% of each frame's image by panning the camera horizontally to follow the 'action'; films like 'Lawrence of Arabia' (2.20:1 aspect ratio) lost crucial visual information that changed the meaning of scenes; the widespread adoption of letterboxing on LaserDisc and then DVD largely ended pan-and-scan by 2005.

The 'drive-in theater' — an outdoor cinema where audiences watch films from their cars using FM radio sound — was invented by Richard Hollingshead and first opened in Camden, New Jersey, on June 6, 1933; at their peak in the late 1950s, over 4,000 drive-ins operated in the United States; fewer than 300 remain, but they have experienced a modest revival as family and nostalgic entertainment venues.

The 'multiplex' cinema format — multiple screening rooms in a single building — was introduced by AMC Theaters in Kansas City in 1963 with the first twin cinema; the subsequent growth to 6, 8, 12, and 18-screen multiplexes economized operations while reducing the communal shared-experience aspect of traditional single-screen cinemas; the industry's pivot to luxury recliners and premium large-format screens from 2010 attempted to compete with home streaming.

The 'Chinese box office' overtook the United States as the world's largest cinema market in 2020 and has remained the largest or second-largest annually since; China's 75,000+ cinema screens (versus 40,000 in the US) have made Chinese audience preferences increasingly central to Hollywood production decisions — particularly avoiding content that could trigger China's opaque censorship system controlling foreign film quotas.

The 'day-and-date' release strategy — releasing films simultaneously in theaters and on streaming/video-on-demand — was forced on studios during the COVID-19 pandemic (2020–2021) when theaters closed; Warner Bros.' controversial decision to release its entire 2021 slate simultaneously on HBO Max without theater chains' consent led to lawsuits and industry restructuring; the subsequent 45-day exclusive theatrical window became the post-pandemic standard.

The 'Christopher Nolan IMAX manifesto' — Nolan's public advocacy for large-format film and theatrical exhibition, articulated in his acceptance speeches, interviews, and the essay 'My Case for Film' — has been credited with convincing Kodak to continue manufacturing film stock and the major studios to maintain theatrical release windows; no other director has been as publicly influential on the film industry's technological choices.

The 'photobook dummy' tradition — creating hand-made mockups of proposed photography books to present to publishers or competitions — has become a significant art form; the Mack First Book Award, Aperture First PhotoBook Award, and Kassel Photobook Festival have elevated the photobook dummy to a competitive field; winners like Nelli Palomäki and Paul Gaffney have launched careers through photobook competition wins before finding publishers.

The 'vernacular photography' category — including family snapshots, vacation photographs, school portraits, passport photos, and surveillance images — was first exhibited seriously by Jonathan Green at the University of California at Riverside (1974); subsequent collections by Joachim Schmid, Erik Kessels, and the Found Photo Foundation treated found photographs as ethnographic documents of everyday life rather than failed art photography.

The 'photofinishing industry' — commercial film processing and printing services — reached its peak in the 1990s when Kodak's wholesale photofinishing network processed over 20 billion prints annually in the United States; the industry's collapse after 2003 eliminated over 100,000 photographic jobs and closed tens of thousands of minilab locations in pharmacies, supermarkets, and dedicated photo shops worldwide.

The 'Photoshop' cultural shift — from professional tool requiring training and expensive hardware to consumer application — occurred when Adobe released Photoshop CS2 for free (accidentally) in 2013 and then normalized subscription pricing through Creative Cloud; 'photoshopping' as a consumer activity (selfie editing, skin smoothing, background replacement) has created a generation that considers post-processing images a natural part of photography.

The 'color grading' workflow in cinema was transformed by DaVinci Resolve, originally a $30,000 professional grading system acquired by Blackmagic Design in 2009 and released as free software in 2014; within five years, DaVinci Resolve became the dominant professional color grading software and is now used on over 70% of theatrical releases, while also being used by YouTube creators for free on their home computers.

The 'first cinema in the world' distinction is contested: the Cinématographe Lumière's December 28, 1895, Paris screening is most commonly cited, but the Skladanowskys' Bioscop in Berlin premiered November 1, 1895; R.W. Paul and Birt Acres had demonstrated film in London in January 1896; and Thomas Edison's Kinetoscope parlors had shown films to paying customers since April 1894 — cinema's 'first' depends on the criteria.

The 'Photo Editor' profession — selecting, sequencing, and captioning photographs for magazines, newspapers, and online platforms — was recognized as a distinct creative discipline by Alexey Brodovitch at Harper's Bazaar (1934–1958); Brodovitch's concept of 'astonish me' as the criterion for selecting photographs, and his systematic training of photographers including Richard Avedon, established the photo editor as a creative force in photography.

The 'Picture Editor' at the New York Times — responsible for selecting which of thousands of daily images appears in print and online — has been described as making more decisions about what Americans see of world events than any other individual in journalism; the Times' photo editing philosophy of seeking 'surprising, authentic, and compositionally excellent' photographs has influenced how photo editors across the industry evaluate work.

The 'cinema of attractions' concept, introduced by film historian Tom Gunning (1986), describes early cinema's primary appeal not as narrative storytelling but as spectacle — the amazement of seeing images move; Gunning argued that this 'attraction' mode persists in contemporary blockbuster cinema's action sequences, CGI spectacles, and musical numbers that temporarily interrupt narrative to deliver pure sensory experience.

The 'intermission' that once divided long films into two halves — permitting audiences to visit bathrooms, purchase refreshments, and give projectionists time to change reels — was standard for films over two hours through the 1960s; 'Ben-Hur' (1959), 'Lawrence of Arabia' (1962), and '2001: A Space Odyssey' (1968) all featured intermissions; the elimination of intermissions from contemporary epic films (including Nolan's 3-hour 'Oppenheimer') has become a source of audience complaint.

source.name: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

text: The 'scratch track' in film production — a rough audio recording made during filming to help editors synchronize picture and sound — is typically replaced by ADR (Automated Dialogue Replacement) or 'looping' in post-production when location sound is unusable; approximately 30–50% of dialogue in major Hollywood films is ADR recorded in studios, though the seamlessness of the process means most viewers never notice.

The 'best boy' film crew position — second-in-command to the gaffer (lighting) or key grip (equipment) — has a disputed etymology; the most credible explanation is that it derives from merchant sailing terminology for the first mate's assistant; 'best boy grip' and 'best boy electric' are now standard above-the-line crew credits whose archaic names reflect cinema's manual-labor craft origins.

source.name: International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees

text: The 'green screen' (chroma key) compositing technique — placing actors in front of a uniformly colored background for later digital replacement — uses green because digital cameras have greater green sensitivity than red or blue, and human skin contains no green tones; the technique's visible failure modes (green spill on hair, edge fringing on transparent objects) have generated entire sub-industries of cleanup software.

The 'matte painting' technique — creating photorealistic painted backgrounds combined with live-action footage — was pioneered by Norman Dawn beginning in 1905; studios employed dedicated matte painting departments through the 1990s, producing landscapes, buildings, and environments impossible to build or find; Disney's 'The Lion King' (1994) included one of the last major traditionally painted matte shots before digital replaced the craft.

The 'model miniature' special effects technique — filming scale models with cameras positioned close to the ground to simulate normal perspective — was used to create explosions, cityscapes, and spacecraft in films from 'Metropolis' (1927) through 'Return of the Jedi' (1983); the ILM team that built and filmed the Death Star trench sequence for 'Star Wars' used a camera tracking system invented specifically for that film.

The 'particle simulation' in CGI — computing the behavior of thousands of individual particles (water drops, sparks, smoke, hair) using physics algorithms — has been a computational frontier since ILM's 'Wrath of Khan' planet Genesis sequence (1982); Weta Digital's water simulation for 'Avatar: The Way of Water' (2022) required months of computation to simulate ocean movement accurately enough to match photographic reference.

The 'Academy Award for Best Visual Effects' has been awarded since the inaugural ceremony in 1929 (then 'Best Engineering Effects'); early winners used optical printing, matte paintings, and miniatures; the 1993 transition to CGI dominance began with 'Jurassic Park'; by 2020 virtually all nominated films were primarily CGI-based, though Christopher Nolan's practical-effects films ('Dunkirk,' 'Tenet') have won nominations using physical rather than computer-generated images.

source.name: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences

text: The 'VFX artist burnout' crisis — characterized by crunch culture, outsourcing to low-wage markets, and commoditization of visual effects work — was brought to public attention when the VFX company Rhythm & Hues declared bankruptcy weeks after their work on 'Life of Pi' won the Academy Award for Best Visual Effects in 2013; workers wearing 'Down with the Academy' t-shirts outside the ceremony became the industry's first visible labor protest.

The 'stunt performer' profession — actors who perform dangerous physical sequences professionally — has been campaigned for Academy Award recognition since 2003; no Oscar category for stunt performance exists despite stunts being among the most technically skilled and physically dangerous work in filmmaking; the Academy's resistance is attributed to difficulty defining 'performance' versus 'choreography' in stunt sequences.

The 'method acting' technique, developed by Konstantin Stanislavski and adapted by Lee Strasberg at the Actor's Studio in New York (1947), emphasizes emotional truth through personal experience recall; extreme method practitioners including Robert De Niro (gaining 60 pounds for 'Raging Bull'), Dustin Hoffman (staying awake for days for 'Marathon Man'), and Daniel Day-Lewis (living as a cobbler for months before 'The Phantom Thread') have made 'method' synonymous with dedicated transformation.

The 'casting couch' term — referring to the implicit exchange of sexual favors for film roles — originated in early Hollywood where studio heads had absolute power over contract players; the post-Weinstein era has produced industry-wide contractual 'intimacy coordinators' (first appearing on television sets around 2018) whose professional role is to choreograph and safeguard intimate scenes — a structural response to decades of abuse.

The 'opening weekend box office' reporting system, in which films' commercial success is judged by their first three-day gross, was established by the Hollywood studios in the 1970s to create news stories driving second-weekend attendance; the competitive 'race' framing of box office results as sports scores has been criticized by directors including Martin Scorsese for reducing complex cultural objects to financial competition.

The 'pre-production' phase of filmmaking — including script development, casting, location scouting, set design, costume design, and visual effects planning — typically lasts 3–6 months for major productions; Stanley Kubrick's pre-production for 'Full Metal Jacket' (1987) lasted over two years; for 'Eyes Wide Shut' (1999) he engaged the actors and began filming before completing the script, conducting pre-production and production simultaneously.

The 'assistant director' (AD) role in film production is primarily logistical rather than creative — managing the shooting schedule, coordinating department heads, maintaining set discipline, and relaying the director's instructions; the First AD creates the 'shooting schedule' (the day-by-day plan of what will be filmed) that determines the entire production's economics, making the AD arguably as important to a film's financial viability as the director.

The 'call sheet' — the daily production document distributed to cast and crew listing each day's filming schedule, location, cast requirements, and crew call times — is the primary management tool of film production; a major studio production's call sheet for a complex action day can run 15+ pages and coordinate hundreds of people, vehicles, equipment packages, and logistics across multiple locations simultaneously.

The 'clapper board' (or 'slate') used at the beginning of each cinema take to synchronize audio and video — marked with scene and take numbers and snapped sharply to create a visible and audible sync point — dates to the earliest days of sound cinema; its format has been standardized by the SMPTE to include production name, scene, take, date, and timecode, enabling editors to organize thousands of takes efficiently.

source.name: Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers

text: Photography and cinema, born within 70 years of each other (1826 and 1895), have together transformed human consciousness more than any other technology — enabling people to see their own faces objectively for the first time, compressing the world's visual diversity into universally accessible form, creating shared cultural experiences across language and geography, and preserving the faces and voices of the dead; as AI-generated imagery challenges the indexical truth claim of both arts, the question of what a photograph or film 'means' is being asked with new urgency, ensuring that both mediums remain philosophically central to human experience.
